summary: Generate global hackathon ideas from diverse angles, shortlist, judge/red-team each, pick a winner
logs: 7 finalists (incl. baseline): Utter: an AAC keyboard that turns a few taps into full sentences, on-device | Telegraph: an AI codec for messages over satellite, SMS and dead zones | Blindfill: the cloud reads the form, only your device reads you | Denominator: adds the missing baseline to every statistic you read | Strangers' Eyes: an AI stalker tries to find you in your photo before you post it | Asking For A Friend: turn your real legal problem into an anonymous hypothetical before any AI sees it | Muganga (baseline)

dropped.name: Formbridge: answer any form in your own language
dropped.reason: Merged into the Blindfill finalist (near-duplicate split: values stay on-device, the public form schema goes to the cloud). Its answer-in-your-own-language flow, Translator API bridge, side panel for HTML forms and iOS letter loop were folded in.

dropped.name: Unsigned: anonymous feedback that is actually anonymous
dropped.reason: The anonymity-set meter is clever, but it is a two-sided HR sale that needs employer buy-in, risks being seen as survey software, and would be a fourth privacy-split finalist.

dropped.name: Tuner
dropped.reason: Bouncer (Imbue) already ships an on-device feed filter for Chrome and iPhone, political examples could put judges off, and the web demo depends on Chrome Nano.

dropped.name: Small Print
dropped.reason: Dark-pattern detectors and terms-of-service summarizers are common, the core relies on Chrome Nano (probably not eligible on the 8 GB M1), and the iOS role is thin.

dropped.name: Beside: a screen helper that can't see your secrets
dropped.reason: Highest build risk (Live API streaming inside an extension in 11 days), the redaction gate depends on Nano, and it overlaps Google's own Gemini in Chrome 'Go Live'.

dropped.name: Easel: Easy Read with pictures for every page and letter
dropped.reason: 'Simplify this page' will be crowded and AI Easy Read prototypes already exist (UK Simply Readable). AI pictogram accuracy is a known problem, and the shared-library twist isn't enough to beat the finalists.

dropped.name: Leakfinder: an audit of any bank, in any country, without Plaid
dropped.reason: Crowded subscription-tracker category (its own write-up rates it weakest on novelty). The demo needs a synthetic bank site, and it depends on Nano for its core value.

dropped.name: WaitTime
dropped.reason: Strong evidence and a global teacher audience, but SpeechTranscriber doesn't run in the iOS Simulator, separating teacher from student speech is unsolved, and classroom noise makes an 11-day demo fragile.

dropped.name: Earshot
dropped.reason: Great demo, but live listening doesn't work in the iOS Simulator, speech recognition on public-address audio is unreliable, and a missed alert is high-stakes. Utter already fills the accessibility slot. Strong alternate if speech feasibility is proven.

dropped.name: Labelwise
dropped.reason: Web-only, which weakens the multi-platform Grand Prize case. It depends entirely on Nano reading tiny icons on an 8 GB M1, and accessibility judges may hear 'overlay'.

dropped.name: Undertone
dropped.reason: Crowded tone-analyzer category, small on-device models are weak at pragmatics, and it carries framing risk for autistic users.

dropped.name: Ibid: confidential citation checker for peer reviewers
dropped.reason: Citation-existence checkers are crowded in 2026, the audience is narrow, and checking claims against abstracts will often return NOT_VERIFIABLE, which weakens the demo.

dropped.name: Kappa: two-coder qualitative analysis
dropped.reason: Clever dual-coder framing, but a niche audience, a demo built on kappa numbers that is hard to make compelling in 3 minutes, a weak iOS role, and unverified Nano throughput on hundreds of responses. Its pattern of two independent readers plus an audit sample was borrowed into Blindfill.

dropped.name: Nanoproof
dropped.reason: A developer tool: the brief penalizes tech demos and its impact is narrow, so it suits a category prize better than the Grand Prize.

dropped.name: Fieldwise: AI double data entry for paper forms
dropped.reason: Mature, crowded document-AI market. Nano's handwriting accuracy is unknown, so the escalation rate could undermine the story, and the demo is less compelling.

dropped.name: FixPack
dropped.reason: Solid and feasible ('cloud compiles, device executes'), but close to existing enterprise service-AI products and 'chat with a PDF'. Telegraph covers the offline slot with a more original split. Best alternate for the sixth slot if the user wants something outside the privacy theme.

dropped.name: Hearthside
dropped.reason: AI game NPCs are a common hackathon theme, the entertainment framing weakens Impact, and polishing a game would consume the 11 days.

dropped.name: Unspoiled
dropped.reason: Crowded spoiler-blocker niche, web-only (no multi-platform), soft impact, and the most dependent of all the ideas on Chrome Nano running on the 8 GB M1.

finalist.name: Utter: an AAC keyboard that turns a few taps into full sentences, on-device
finalist.merged_from: Utter (accessibility-inclusion lens). Also takes the idea of on-device captioning of what the conversation partner says, which Earshot uses too.
finalist.pitch:
USER: People worldwide who can't speak or speak very little: ALS/MND, cerebral palsy, minimally verbal autism, aphasia after a stroke, and temporary loss of speech after intubation or laryngectomy. Also the families and speech therapists who set up their devices. About 97M people may benefit from AAC (augmentative and alternative communication; Beukelman & Light 2020). The devices are the same everywhere: iPads at home, Chromebooks at school.

PROBLEM: Conversation runs at 120-180 words per minute. AAC users who type letter by letter or by eye gaze reach 8-10, so partners walk away, finish their sentences for them, or only ask yes/no questions. Google Research's SpeakFaster (Nature Communications 2024) showed that an LLM expanding abbreviated input saves 57% of motor actions and makes ALS users 29-60% faster. It stayed a cloud prototype built on a fine-tuned model. Mainstream AAC apps (Proloquo2Go, TD Snap, Avaz) still use symbol grids and word prediction.

ON-DEVICE JOB: Generates sentences at typing speed. Each tap sends three things to the on-device model: the user's keywords or partial words ('tird bk hurt'), the partner's last utterance, and a style card of 300 tokens or less. The model returns 4 candidate sentences. On iOS this is Apple Foundation Models through HybridModel with a prewarmed session, returning numbered lines or a suggest(...) tool call, because structured output isn't available on-device on iOS yet. On web it is Gemini Nano, single-turn, with JSON-schema output. 'Reply mode' offers 4 one-tap answers to the partner's question before the user types anything. The partner's speech is captioned by the operating system's on-device speech recognition (Chrome Web Speech with processLocally; SFSpeechRecognizer on iOS), and the app speaks through on-device TTS (Personal Voice on real devices). WHY ON-DEVICE: a cloud round trip on every keystroke breaks turn-taking. Every word passes through this model and is literally the person's voice, including pain, toileting and intimacy. An AAC device that needs Wi-Fi leaves someone unable to speak in a hospital bed or on a bus. And thousands of generations a day cost nothing locally.

CLOUD JOB: Rare, deeper work. (1) Persona builder: long-context Gemini condenses pasted writing (old emails, posts, a life story) into the small style card that goes into every on-device prompt. This makes a small model that hasn't been fine-tuned sound like the person. (2) Situation boards: before 'dentist tomorrow' or 'grandson's birthday', the cloud writes about 30 likely phrases and questions, cached offline with Firestore persistence. (3) Expressive Gemini TTS in many languages when online, with on-device TTS as the fallback. Stretch goal: generated picture symbols for children, since commercial symbol sets are licensed and expensive.

DEMO MOMENT: An iPad (Simulator) in airplane mode with an 'on-device, 0 bytes sent' badge. The partner asks 'How are you feeling after the surgery?' and live captions show it. The user taps 'tird bk hurt'. Four sentences appear, the first being 'I'm tired and my back still hurts. Can you help me sit up?' One tap speaks it. A counter reads 'Utter: 12 taps / typing it: 58 taps'. Cut to a caregiver in Chrome preparing a 'dentist tomorrow' board in the cloud, which appears on the iPad through Firestore.

PLATFORMS: iOS/iPadOS is the primary platform; Foundation Models runs in the iOS Simulator on this M1. A Chrome web app covers Chromebooks in special-education classrooms and doubles as the caregiver dashboard, using Nano where available and the cloud otherwise. Android works through the cloud path.

FIREBASE: AI Logic hybrid inference (PREFER_ON_DEVICE for prediction; ONLY_IN_CLOUD for the persona, boards and TTS). App Check (App Attest, the debug provider in the Simulator, reCAPTCHA Enterprise on web). Auth (the user and caregiver share one profile). Firestore with offline persistence (style card, boards, phrase history). Remote Config (prompt templates, number of candidates, few-shot examples, TTS flag). Hosting.

KEY RISKS: (1) A small model is weak at expanding bare initials. Lead with keywords and partial words, and add few-shot examples, the style card and a re-rank from local phrase history. (2) Agency and ethics: the app never speaks automatically and every candidate can be edited. (3) Live partner captions and Personal Voice may not work in the Simulator, so show captions on web and the core typing flow on iOS.
finalist.why_finalist: Rank 1. It scores well on all four criteria at once. The reasons to run on-device (typing-speed latency, how intimate the user's words are, needing to work offline) are the textbook case for hybrid inference, and the device genuinely can't do the cloud's jobs (long-context persona, situation boards, expressive TTS). The impact is specific, backed by evidence and global. It turns Google Research's own SpeakFaster prototype into a product, which Google judges are likely to recognize. Very few of the 3,200+ entrants will build AAC. The iOS on-device path can be fully tested in the Simulator on the 8 GB M1, so the multi-platform story doesn't depend on Chrome Nano. It is a communication tool, not a clinical one, which answers the user's concern about leaning toward health.

judge.rationale:
This is one of the few pitches in the pile where hybrid inference is the reason the product works, not a feature added on. Every reason for on-device holds up on its own: a model call on every tap, so a cloud round trip breaks turn-taking; words that are literally the person's voice, including toileting and intimacy, so privacy matters; offline use in a hospital bed or on a bus; and thousands of free generations a day. The cloud side does the rare, heavy work: condensing long writing into a style card, building situation boards ahead of time, and expressive TTS. The best pattern here is the cloud teaching the device through a small style card, which lets a small model that hasn't been fine-tuned sound like the person. That is the kind of non-obvious use the Quality of Idea criterion asks for. Building on SpeakFaster (Google Research, Nature Communications 2024) gives a Google panel a credible starting point and a metric it already knows (motor actions saved). Shipping Web plus iOS, with Firestore boards syncing from caregiver to user, also qualifies for the Grand Prize's multi-platform consideration.

Why it doesn't score higher:
- Tech (7): Apple's roughly 3B on-device model running in the Simulator on an 8 GB M1 will likely take 1.5 to 4 seconds to produce 4 full candidates once you count prefill of the style card and few-shot examples. That isn't "typing speed" unless you stream candidate 1 first and keep prompts small. iOS also has no on-device structured output, so you're parsing numbered lines, which is fragile. Most judges trying the hosted web app won't have Nano, so they'll get the cloud path, which is the experience the pitch says is wrong for AAC. The "0 bytes sent" badge also has to cover only inference, because Firestore, App Check and Remote Config traffic will make it false otherwise.
- Design (7): The two-sided product (user keyboard, caregiver dashboard, Reply mode, the tap counter) holds together. But real AAC users with ALS often use eye gaze or switch scanning, not taps. Without dwell- and scan-friendly targets and visible support for iPadOS Eye Tracking or Switch Control, an SLP judge will see a keyboard demo, not an AAC product.
- Impact (8): A specific, global audience, the same devices everywhere, a research-backed problem, and an outcome you can measure. What's missing is any validation with an actual AAC user or speech-language pathologist, and the risk of putting words in someone's mouth needs more than "never auto-speaks." It needs to be visible in the UX.
- Idea (8): Far from the summarizer and chatbot crowd, but LLM-powered AAC is not new to Google judges (SpeakFaster, Project Relate, several entries in the Gemma impact challenges). What's novel is doing it on-device and hybrid with a cloud-built persona, not the category itself.

Executed well, this belongs in the top 1-2% of the field and is a realistic Grand Prize or runner-up contender.
judge.biggest_weakness: Nothing in the plan proves the core loop works: that a small, untuned on-device model turns terse input like 'tird bk hurt' into good sentences fast enough to beat typing. Judges will see it only in a Simulator video that could be cherry-picked, while the hosted app they try runs mostly in the cloud, which contradicts the pitch's own reason for being on-device. If the expansions are mediocre or take 3 seconds, the whole case falls apart, and no real AAC user or SLP is involved to show otherwise.
judge.best_upgrade: Replace claims with evidence. Build a small, reproducible benchmark in the repo and in the app, using the openly released dialogue corpus from SpeakFaster ('Turk Dialogues') or a few hundred abbreviated AAC-style turns. Report keystroke savings rate, top-1 and top-4 accuracy, and p50/p95 latency for four setups: on-device with the style card, on-device without it, cloud, and the hybrid fallback. Show a live 'taps saved / ms / ON_DEVICE vs IN_CLOUD' strip on every generation, and put the comparison table at the start of the video. This one change makes the Tech score a measured result instead of a hope, shows the style card is worth having, gives the Impact case a SpeakFaster-style number that judges trust, and lets judges without on-device models still see what the on-device path achieves. If there's time, add a 20-second clip of one speech-language pathologist or AAC user trying it.

fatal_flaws: The core idea has already been built and rewarded, including by Google. 'AAC Board AI' won 'Most helpful application' in Google's Chrome Built-in AI Challenge 2025: an on-device, offline AAC app built on Chrome's built-in AI (developer.chrome.com/blog/ai-challenge-winners-2025; devpost.com/software/aac-board-ai). Judges from the same ecosystem may see 'on-device AI for nonspeaking people' as a repeat. That undercuts the 'non-obvious' part of Quality of Idea.

Reply mode and live partner captions are not new either. The open-source SpeakEasy (github.com/enzomar/speakeasy) already runs on-device Whisper to transcribe the partner's speech and a Qwen3 model over WebGPU to suggest 5 replies, in the browser and on iOS/Android via Capacitor. FreeSpoke Local (dev.to, a Hacktoberfest entry) turns 2-3 keywords into Quick/Full/Question speech cards offline with Qwen2.5-3B, with JSON output. AbilityMic is already in the App Store as an AAC app using on-device Apple Intelligence for sentence completion. Tobii Dynavox, the market leader, ships AI phrase prediction in TD Talk (demoed at the Microsoft Ability Summit in 2025). The only clearly new pieces left are the cloud-built persona style card and caregiver boards synced across devices.

The iOS on-device model may refuse the exact content AAC exists for. Apple Developer Forums report model-level refusals (LanguageModelError 'may contain sensitive content') for health terms on iOS 27 betas (threads 836673 and 857739, the second about grief text). In those reports, `.permissiveContentTransformations` did not help, and guardrails do not apply to guided generation. The Firebase HybridModel docs do not say whether guardrails can be configured, or whether a refusal falls back to the cloud. Phrases like 'need toilet', 'catheter hurts', 'I want to die' and intimacy are core AAC vocabulary. A refusal leaves the user unable to speak. A silent cloud fallback breaks the '0 bytes sent' promise.

The iOS demo platform is unverified on this exact machine. The host runs macOS 26.6.2 with Xcode 27.2, and the only installed Simulator runtime is iOS 27.0. The Simulator uses the host Mac's Foundation Models, and it is unverified whether an iOS 27 Simulator works with macOS 26 model assets; one source suggests it needs a macOS 27 host. If it doesn't work, the plan's primary platform loses its on-device demo. The fix is either a large iOS 26.x runtime download or a macOS upgrade on an 8 GB machine, both late in an 11-day build.

The 'Chromebooks in special-education classrooms' claim is false for the on-device path. Chrome's docs limit Gemini Nano on ChromeOS to Chromebook Plus models, and they require 22 GB of free disk plus more than 4 GB of VRAM, or 16 GB of RAM. A 2025 Chromium report says on-device Web Speech was disabled on ChromeOS. On typical school Chromebooks every keystroke would go to the cloud, which contradicts the privacy pitch for the audience the brief names.

The latency argument is backwards. 'A cloud round trip on every keystroke breaks turn-taking' assumes on-device is faster. Producing 4 candidates means roughly 100+ output tokens after a prefill of 600-900 tokens (style card, few-shot examples, partner utterance). That can easily take longer on Nano on an M1 or on Apple FM than Gemini Flash-Lite takes in the cloud. Producing candidates 'at typing speed' on every tap is not credible, so it has to be debounced. A judge who compares the two could see on-device as the slower path.

The privacy story contradicts itself. Cloud Gemini TTS sends every spoken sentence to Google. The persona builder uploads private emails and a life story. If Nano isn't eligible, PREFER_ON_DEVICE quietly sends everything to the cloud. The '0 bytes sent' badge is true only in airplane mode, and the design never handles that tension.

The headline metric overstates the savings. The input 'tird bk hurt' became 'I'm tired and my back still hurts. Can you help me sit up?', which adds a request and the word 'still' that the user never typed. Counting 58 versus 12 taps credits the model for invented content, which is the 'words put in my mouth' problem the AAC community worries about. SpeakFaster's 57% figure came from a fine-tuned 64B LaMDA trained on about 1.8M triplets. An un-fine-tuned model of roughly 3B parameters will be clearly worse, especially with initials.

There is too much scope for one agent on an 8 GB M1 in 11 days. The plan covers a SwiftUI AAC keyboard, speech capture, TTS, Auth, App Check through App Attest or the debug provider, Firestore offline, Remote Config, a web keyboard, a caregiver dashboard, reCAPTCHA Enterprise, Hosting, the persona builder, boards and Gemini TTS, plus symbol generation as a stretch goal. Running the Xcode Simulator's Foundation Models, Chrome's 4 GB Nano model and the agent at the same time will push the machine into heavy swapping.
red.existing_competitors:
These projects already do much of what Utter proposes.
- AAC Board AI won 'Most helpful application' in Google's Chrome Built-in AI Challenge 2025. It is an on-device, offline AAC app built on Chrome's built-in AI, using the Translator API and IndexedDB, with the Prompt API listed as a next step (developer.chrome.com/blog/ai-challenge-winners-2025, devpost.com/software/aac-board-ai).
- SpeakEasy is an open-source AAC app (github.com/enzomar/speakeasy). It runs Qwen3 0.6B/1.7B or Gemma 3 1B over WebGPU, plus on-device Whisper for its 'Listen Mode', which transcribes the partner and suggests 5 replies. It works on web and iOS/Android and supports 10 languages. That is essentially Utter's reply mode, built with no cloud.
- FreeSpoke Local (dev.to, a Hacktoberfest AI challenge entry) runs Qwen2.5-3B offline. It turns 2-3 keywords into JSON with Quick/Full/Question speech cards and speaks them with Web Speech TTS.
- AbilityMic (Product Hunt) is an App Store AAC app. It uses on-device Apple Intelligence for smart suggestions and sentence completion, and it adds AI board/symbol generation and HomeKit.
- Tobii Dynavox TD Talk is from the market leader. It has AI phrase prediction that adapts to the user's style, demoed at the Microsoft Ability Summit in March 2025, and uses Azure neural voices.
- Spoken (Tap to Talk AAC) offers AI next-word prediction that learns from the user and adapts to location.
- Cboard is open-source (GPL). It has an AI sentence feature and an OpenAI-based 'AI Board Builder' that generates boards from a theme, which overlaps with Utter's situation boards.
- FreeSpeech AAC (Merkie, MIT license) is open-source and uses GPT for phrase conjugation.
- Research: Google's SpeakFaster (Nature Communications 2024; fine-tuned LaMDA; cloud), KWickChat (keywords to sentences, 2022), the 'Design Probes for AI-Driven AAC' aphasia study (2025: intention plus 2-4 keywords produces 3 GPT sentences), SocializeChat (2025: a GPT-based AAC tool grounded in personal memories, close to the persona card), and Talk For Me (an alpha iOS app using an LLM to generate sentences).
- Neither Apple (May 2026 accessibility announcement) nor Google has shipped a first-party LLM AAC product, so the space is still open at the platform level.
- Note: I hit the web-search budget before I could check the #BuildHybridAI gallery itself or recent AAC ethics literature.
red.mitigations:
This is a keep-with-conditions verdict. Utter moves from risky to viable only if the Day-1 spikes below pass.

1. Day-1 spikes, before any UI work
   - (a) Call `SystemLanguageModel.default` availability through the Firebase HybridModel (v12.13.0 or later) in the iOS 27.0 Simulator on this macOS 26.6.2 host. The Mac does have the UAF_FM_GenerativeModels assets. If the model is unavailable, download an iOS 26.x Simulator runtime right away, or make the web app the primary platform.
   - (b) Run a red-team set of about 60 AAC-sensitive inputs through both Apple FM and Chrome Nano and log refusals. Use toileting, catheter, pain, end-of-life/'I want to die', sexuality and swearing.
   - (c) Measure time-to-first-candidate and time for all 4 candidates on Nano (M1) and FM (Simulator) against Flash-Lite in the cloud.
   - Note: Chrome's OptGuideOnDeviceModel (4.0 GB, version 2025.8.8.1141) and the SODA speech packs are already on this Mac, so the web on-device path is likely OK.
2. Refusal handling. Never fall back to the cloud silently on a refusal. Instead:
   - offer an on-device non-LLM path: speak the keywords verbatim, use template expansion, and pull from local phrase history;
   - show an explicit per-utterance 'Send to cloud?' choice;
   - pre-screen inputs and keep sensitive core phrases (toilet, pain, suction, reposition) as fixed, editable quick-phrases that never touch a model.
3. Reframe 'why on-device' around privacy, offline use and zero marginal cost, not latency. Publish measured numbers honestly. Debounce generation on a pause of about 300 ms. Stream the first candidate (the faithful literal expansion) before the 3 that add content.
4. Fix the honesty of the metric and the agency model.
   - Candidate 1 must use only the user's words. Visually mark any word the AI added.
   - Count saved taps only against the sentence the user accepted, and log edits.
   - Never speak automatically.
5. Differentiate explicitly. Name AAC Board AI, SpeakEasy, FreeSpoke, AbilityMic and SpeakFaster as prior art in the write-up. The pitch should be that the cloud distills who you are (persona style card, caregiver-prepared boards) and the device speaks for you privately. Lead the demo with the 'sounds like me' contrast: the same keywords, with and without the style card.
6. Fix the privacy contradictions.
   - On-device TTS is the default. Gemini TTS is an opt-in 'expressive' toggle, labeled as cloud.
   - The persona builder runs once, with explicit consent, and produces a style card the user can read and edit.
   - When Nano or FM is not eligible, show a visible 'cloud mode' banner and ask for opt-in, or fall back to classic word prediction.
   - Drop the claim about on-device use on school Chromebooks. Say Chrome on desktop and Chromebook Plus.
7. Cut scope hard.
   - Platforms: iPad (iOS) plus one web app that shares the prompt spec through Remote Config and also hosts the caregiver dashboard.
   - Drop: Android, symbol generation, suggest() tool calling, and Personal Voice in the demo.
   - Use numbered-line parsing on iOS and JSON schema on web.
   - Firestore offline sync for boards and the style card is the single cross-device 'wow'.
8. Credibility and practice. Get one quote from a speech-language pathologist or an AAC user. Show big targets that work with dwell or switch scanning, and briefly show iPadOS Switch Control or Eye Tracking. On 8 GB, never run the Simulator's FM and Chrome Nano at the same time; record each demo segment separately.

demo.storyboard:
Total length 3:00. Use an everyday family scene, not a hospital, so the video does not read as another health app. The user already pushed back on that. Film the iOS Simulator inside an iPad bezel and the web app in Chrome. A small "router HUD" stays on screen the whole time and logs each call, for example "suggest > on-device 210ms", "persona > cloud (long context)" or "board > cloud, cached offline". This makes the hybrid inference visible, which is what judging criterion 1 scores.

BEAT 1 (0:00-0:20) THE GAP. Black screen. A cursor types "I-'-m-..." one letter at a time, sped up to show eye-gaze typing at 8-10 words per minute. Off screen, a grandson asks "Grandpa, are you coming to my match Saturday?" and waits... then says "...never mind, I'll ask Mum." Title cards: "Conversation: about 150 words/min. Typing with your eyes: 8." and "97M people may need AAC." Cite SpeakFaster (Nature Comms 2024) in small type. Do not imply any Google affiliation.

BEAT 2 (0:20-0:55) SPEED AND REPLY MODE. iPad with the Mac's Wi-Fi visibly off in the menu bar, an in-app "Offline" pill, and a badge reading "On-device. Nothing sent." The partner's question appears as a caption. Before the user types anything, Reply mode offers 4 one-tap answers: "Yes, I'll be there!" / "What time?" / "Not sure yet" / "Can you push my chair there?" The user wants something warmer and taps "prd wont miss". Four sentences stream in, a millisecond timer is visible, and the first reads "I'm so proud of you, I wouldn't miss it for the world." One tap speaks it. A counter shows Utter taps vs. full typing; use the real measured counts. Voiceover: "A cloud call on every keystroke breaks turn-taking. So this runs on the device, offline and free, thousands of times a day."

BEAT 3 (0:55-1:30) SAME TAPS, TWO VOICES. This is the non-obvious idea and should be the memorable shot. In Chrome, the daughter pastes Grandpa's old emails into Persona Builder. The HUD flips to "CLOUD: long context, runs once". Gemini condenses them into a style card of 300 tokens or less, shown on screen with lines like "dry humour, says 'champion', signs off 'love, G'". Split screen: the same input "prd wont miss" now produces Grandpa's voice ("Wouldn't miss it, champion.") next to a teenage user's persona ("ofc I'm coming!! so proud"). Voiceover: "The cloud listens once. The device sounds like you all day."

BEAT 4 (1:30-1:55) SITUATION BOARDS. The caregiver types "dentist tomorrow" and Gemini writes about 30 phrases, which sync to the iPad through Firestore. Cut to Wi-Fi off "next day": the board is still there, and on-device generation mixes its phrases into suggestions. Show one candidate being edited before it is spoken, to make agency visible: nothing is ever spoken automatically.

BEAT 5 (1:55-2:25) ANY CHROMEBOOK, ANY LANGUAGE. Classroom framing in the Chrome web app. On a machine with Nano, the badge reads "Gemini Nano" and the DevTools Network tab stays empty during generation. On a machine without Nano, the same UI shows "Cloud fallback". A "Never send my words" toggle switches to ONLY_ON_DEVICE. Do a quick switch to Spanish: the style card and suggestions both work. When online, expressive Gemini TTS speaks; offline, the device voice takes over.

BEAT 6 (2:25-2:45) HOW IT WORKS. One diagram card. Per keystroke: on-device (private, offline, zero cost). Rare: cloud (persona, boards, expressive TTS). The Firebase stack: AI Logic hybrid, App Check, Auth with a shared caregiver profile, Firestore offline, Remote Config for prompts and candidate count. Show one measured stat from your own test session, such as "1,412 on-device generations, 3 cloud calls".

BEAT 7 (2:45-3:00) CALLBACK. Back to the grandson. This time the reply arrives in seconds, he grins, and he stays in the conversation. Title: "Utter. Your words, at the speed of conversation." Hosted URL, then "Try it in Chrome (no install)".

PRODUCTION NOTES: Record each beat separately. An 8 GB M1 running Xcode, the Simulator, Chrome and a screen recorder at once will stutter. Use Network Link Conditioner or turn Wi-Fi off, because the Simulator has no airplane mode. Voice the partner with a real person. Do not perform a disability on camera.
demo.weak_spots:
1) The core promise weakens on the hosted URL. A judge whose Chrome has no Nano gets cloud round trips of about 0.7-1.5 s, which undercuts "speed of conversation". Fixes:
- Generate on word boundaries with a debounce, and stream the first candidate.
- Show instant suggestions from local phrase history while the model works.
- Show the inference source honestly.
- Add a JUDGE MODE: anonymous Auth, two preloaded personas, a "play partner question" button so no mic is needed, and a sample-text button in Persona Builder.
Without Judge Mode, tryability drops to about 5. The iOS build is effectively out of reach for judges unless you pay for TestFlight with a public link and pass beta review (1-2 days). Start that by day 7 or skip it.

2) Offline is hard to show in the Simulator. It has no airplane mode and shares the Mac's network. Prove offline with the Mac's Wi-Fi off, an in-app NWPathMonitor pill, and the Network tab on web. Check that the iOS HybridModel can report which model answered. If it can't, instrument it yourself. A badge saying "0 bytes sent" must be literally true per generation, and Firestore, App Check and Analytics all make network calls.

3) It is still health-adjacent. The user explicitly questioned leaning on health. The pitch's "after surgery" and "back hurts" demo lines pull it back into medicine. Present it as communication and accessibility for everyday life (family, school, work), and keep the medical uses to one sentence.

4) The small model is weak at expanding bare initials, and judges will try hard inputs. Make keywords and partial words the main input, use few-shot examples from Remote Config, and never claim parity with SpeakFaster. Pre-test the demo inputs and include one edit or reject so a miss looks like a designed feature.

5) Judges may see it as "smart reply for disabled people", which sits in a crowded smart-reply space. The persona style card ("same taps, two voices") and Reply mode are the differentiators. They must land by 1:30 or the idea scores as obvious.

6) Authenticity and ethics. No real AAC user appears in the video and there was no co-design. An LLM putting words in someone's mouth is a known AAC criticism. Mitigate with:
- Visible editing.
- No auto-speak.
- A caregiver/speech-therapist setup flow.
- An honest "next step: co-design with AAC users" line.
- If possible, a consented quote from a speech therapist.

7) The global claim has limits. On-device language coverage is narrow: English-first, with Apple FM and Nano covering only a handful of languages. Many AAC users in low-income settings use cheap Android devices without Nano, which pushes them onto the paid cloud path that needs data. State this plainly, and present Gemini TTS plus the style card as the multilingual path.

8) Input realism. Real users often use switch scanning or eye gaze, not taps. Call the counter "motor actions", support large targets, and test that iOS Switch Control can reach the candidates.

9) Scope is too big for 11 days solo. Cut symbol generation. Prioritise in this order:
- Days 1-4: web core loop with cloud fallback.
- Days 5-8: iOS core loop.
- Days 9-10: persona builder and boards with Firestore sync.
- Day 11: video.
Live partner captions are a nice-to-have. Show them on web only, since the Simulator mic and Personal Voice are unreliable.

10) Hardware risk. Nano in Chrome on an 8 GB M1 is unverified, and Chrome's hardware gate may block it. If it is blocked, the video's on-device web shot is lost and the on-device story rests only on iOS. Test on day 1.

11) Cost and abuse on the hosted URL. Per-keystroke cloud fallback is exposed to the public. Enforce App Check (reCAPTCHA Enterprise), rate-limit, and add a Remote Config kill switch.

finalist.name: Telegraph: an AI codec for messages over satellite, SMS and dead zones
finalist.pitch:
USER: People who can only send short texts. That includes hikers, sailors, overlanders and rural workers in dead zones, now that ordinary phones can text by satellite (Apple/Globalstar, Starlink Direct-to-Cell partners, Skylo). It includes people living through internet shutdowns, where mobile data is cut but SMS often keeps working (Access Now counted at least 313 shutdowns in 52 countries in 2025), and Garmin inReach and Meshtastic LoRa users with 160-230 byte limits. The receivers are families, expedition bases and search-and-rescue coordinators. It works the same in every country.

PROBLEM: On constrained links every character costs time, money and battery. inReach caps messages at 160 characters, and Apple says a satellite message takes at least 15 seconds under a clear sky. Apple built custom compression and a structured questionnaire, but only for Emergency SOS. Everyday messages ramble, get split, and lose the key facts (how many people, needs, ETA, location). Replies from home arrive long, anxious and chopped up.

ON-DEVICE JOB (sender side, which has no internet by definition): turns free text or dictation into a fixed schema: status, people, needs, ETA, destination, battery, hazards, plus a short remainder. Deterministic code packs it into readable ASCII of 160 characters or less, with the location as a Plus Code. On iOS, a Foundation Models multi-turn session asks for missing fields offline ('How many are with you?') and outputs the fields through a packMessage(...) tool call; function calling works on-device, structured output doesn't yet. On web it uses ONLY_ON_DEVICE with a JSON schema. As a round-trip check, the device decodes its own frame back into prose so the sender sees exactly how it will be read. When a compressed reply arrives by SMS, the phone expands it offline into a plain checklist.

CLOUD JOB (receiver side, which is connected): Gemini decodes the frame into a full briefing in the receiver's language. Google Search grounding adds what the sender's phone can't know: forecast and storm timing at that Plus Code, sunset, nearest hut or ranger station, ferry status. It suggests questions to ask back. It also does the hard half of compression: squeezing a 700-character worried reply into one 160-character frame that follows the shared codebook. Thread history lives in Firestore.

DEMO MOMENT: Split screen. On the left, an iPhone Simulator in airplane mode with a 'Satellite only, 160 chars' banner. The user enters a 480-character rambling message and taps Telegraph. A red byte meter drops to a green 128 characters, with an ON-DEVICE badge and a 'they will read:' preview. On the right, the partner's web dashboard receives the frame, and the cloud expands it into a card with a map pin, a grounded 'Storm front reaches this ridge around 16:00, descend now', and suggested replies. The partner types a long reply, the cloud compresses it to 152 characters, and the offline phone expands it into a 4-step checklist.

PLATFORMS: iOS sender (primary; on-device multi-turn plus tool calling, testable in the Simulator). Web: the receiver dashboard on cloud Gemini, plus a Chrome PWA sender that uses Nano where available and falls back to deterministic form-based packing when offline without Nano. Android works through the cloud path.

FIREBASE: AI Logic hybrid inference (iOS HybridModel; web ONLY_ON_DEVICE for packing and ONLY_IN_CLOUD for decoding, enrichment and reply compression). Gemini with Google Search grounding. Remote Config (shared codebook and schema version plus few-shot examples, cached offline so both ends agree, and tunable without an app release). Firestore (threads and family circles, with offline persistence). Auth. App Check. Optional Cloud Functions plus an SMS-gateway webhook for inbound frames. Hosting.

KEY RISKS: (1) A real satellite send can't be shown live, and third-party iOS apps can't send over satellite directly. Send through the share sheet or Messages, demo over SMS, and present satellite as the target link. (2) Lossy compression can change meaning; mitigate with the deterministic schema, the round-trip preview and a facts-only mode. (3) It must never present itself as a replacement for SOS: always route emergencies to official SOS. (4) Getting replies back into the app has friction: use paste or a share extension, and treat a Twilio inbound number as optional (about one extra day of work). (5) Apple already compresses satellite messages, so stress structure, working across channels, enrichment and reply compression rather than byte savings.
finalist.why_finalist: Rank 2. It has the most original hybrid architecture in the pool: the two tiers sit at opposite ends of the wire. Running on-device isn't a preference here; it's physically required, because the sender has no internet. The cloud's enrichment (grounded weather and terrain, translation, reply compression) is only possible on the connected end. This turns the brief's obvious 'offline summarizer' example into a two-way codec, which is the kind of non-obvious use the Quality of Idea criterion rewards. It is global by construction (satellite texting is spreading, shutdowns happen in dozens of countries, and Garmin/LoRa users are everywhere), unlikely to be a common entry, and feasible: the iOS sender runs in the Simulator and the receiver is a cloud web app that works for every judge.

judge.rationale:
After about 300 summarizers, chatbots and scam detectors, this is one of the few entries where the hybrid split comes from the problem itself. The sender is offline by definition, so the model has to run on-device. The receiver is connected, so the cloud is the natural place for grounding and heavy compression. That framing alone puts it in my top tier on Quality of Idea (8). Calling it a 'codec' is creative, and nobody else in the pool is doing it. It is also clearly global, with no regional lock-in.

TECH (7): This is not a toy wrapper. It uses a multi-turn Foundation Models session on iOS that asks for missing fields and emits a packMessage tool call, which is a sophisticated use of what iOS can do on-device. It adds deterministic packing with Plus Codes, a round-trip decode check, a Remote Config codebook cached offline so both ends agree, Firestore offline persistence, and Search grounding on the receiver. What holds it back: the sender runs ONLY_ON_DEVICE and the receiver runs ONLY_IN_CLOUD. That is two fixed modes, not runtime hybrid routing, so the SDK's signature fallback behaviour is barely exercised. A judge scoring 'how effectively it uses hybrid inference' will notice. A lot of the real work is deterministic code rather than the model. Chrome Nano on an 8 GB M1 is also unproven, so the web sender may end up on the form fallback in the demo.

DESIGN (7): The split-screen demo is excellent. The byte meter going from red to green, the ON-DEVICE badge, the 'they will read:' preview and the reply that expands into a checklist all make a coherent product story, not a proof of concept. What holds it back: the satellite link can't be shown, so replies come back by paste or a share extension, which feels staged. It also asks the viewer to follow two apps and two users in three minutes.

IMPACT (6): The audience is real and the numbers are specific (inReach's 160-character cap, Apple's 15-second minimum, 313 shutdowns in 52 countries). But the headline pain, 'my satellite text rambles', is moderate. Real backcountry users already write tersely and use Garmin presets. Apple already compresses and structures satellite messages for SOS. The internet-shutdown angle has more urgency, but it serves a different user (activists and families, not hikers) and is underdeveloped here. The grounded 'descend now' advice is the wow moment, but it is also a safety liability that a careful judge will raise.
judge.biggest_weakness: The hero on-device job, squeezing a hiker's rambling 480-character message into 160 characters, solves a pain judges can wave away with 'just type shorter, or use Garmin presets or Apple's satellite messaging'. The demo can't show the real constrained link, so the impact looks like a clever staged codec rather than a felt problem. The most valuable part, grounded hazard and route intelligence, sits only on the cloud side. It also carries safety risk if AI advice to someone in the backcountry is wrong. On top of that, the fixed ONLY_ON_DEVICE and ONLY_IN_CLOUD modes mean the SDK's hybrid fallback is hardly shown.
judge.best_upgrade: Make the downlink the hero ('the cloud thinks, the phone unpacks') and prove it with a real SMS round trip. The connected receiver side uses Gemini plus Search grounding to turn information the hiker can't reach (weather window at that Plus Code, bail-out route, nearest shelter, ferry status) into a 160-character codebook frame, sent as a real SMS through a Twilio webhook. The phone, really in airplane mode, expands it on-device into a checklist and map annotations. The sender can then ask follow-up questions ('which way is the hut?'), answered offline by the on-device multi-turn session using only the frame and the cached codebook, with a visible 'from frame' citation for every fact. This is value nobody gets by typing shorter. It makes on-device inference do non-trivial work offline, adds a facts-only guardrail against hallucinated safety advice, and removes the 'staged' objection in the video.

fatal_flaws: The 160-character problem is shrinking on the very products judges know. Garmin inReach Messenger Plus allows 1,600-character texts plus photos and voice memos. ZOLEO allows 900 characters. T-Mobile T-Satellite (Starlink) now carries app data such as WhatsApp, Google Maps and AccuWeather on 60+ phones, and iMessage via satellite is reportedly about 500 characters. Only legacy inReach units (about 154 usable chars), plain satellite SMS and Meshtastic (about 200 bytes) keep a hard limit. A demo built on a red-to-green byte meter can look like it solves yesterday's problem.

The on-device AI is missing for the audience the pitch leans on. Apple Foundation Models needs an iPhone 15 Pro or newer with Apple Intelligence on (not mainland China, limited languages). Chrome docs say Gemini Nano APIs are NOT supported on Chrome for Android or iOS, and desktop needs >4 GB VRAM or 16 GB RAM. Android Nano is flagship-only and validated in English and Korean only. People in internet shutdowns (Iran, Uganda, Myanmar, Ethiopia) mostly carry mid-range Android phones. Without a local model and without cloud they get only the deterministic form, so the AI is absent exactly where the impact story is told.

The web on-device sender is decorative: it is laptop-only and nobody texts by satellite from a laptop. That leaves each platform in a single mode. iOS is effectively ONLY_ON_DEVICE, because HybridModel's cloud secondary can't be reached in the offline case it exists for. Web is ONLY_IN_CLOUD. Neither platform shows the SDK actually routing between tiers, so judges scoring 'how effectively it uses hybrid inference' may see two one-tier apps rather than one hybrid app.

It is hard to show why the AI is needed. The plan's own fallback (a 7-field form plus deterministic packing) does the core job. Garmin, ZOLEO and Bivy already ship preset check-ins with GPS. Apple Writing Tools 'Concise' and 'Summary' already shorten text on-device, system-wide, on exactly the devices that have Foundation Models. A sharp judge will ask: why not a form?

The grounded safety advice is risky. Google Search grounding is not a hyperlocal forecast at a Plus Code, and Maps grounding returns places, not weather or ferry status. An LLM line like 'Storm front reaches this ridge around 16:00, descend now' is a hallucination-prone safety directive. It undercuts the 'never replace SOS' position, and SAR-minded judges will penalize it.

The demo's key step, the hop from phone to home, can't happen as shown. The iOS Simulator cannot send SMS (MFMessageComposeViewController.canSendText is false), third-party apps cannot use the satellite link, and a phone in airplane mode cannot write to Firestore. The frame 'arriving' on the dashboard is therefore staged, and judges notice that kind of magic. A Twilio loop that sends replies back to a US number needs A2P 10DLC or toll-free verification, which often takes longer than the 11 days left.

Pitching to people in internet shutdowns while sending plaintext SMS is a safety problem. A machine-parseable frame with a Plus Code location, head count and needs is easy for state surveillance to read in exactly the countries cited. Adding encryption breaks the 'readable ASCII' promise and costs bytes (base64/base85 overhead). The plan doesn't address this contradiction.

The core mechanic has prior art. EchoSign (CXC 2026 hackathon) already uses Gemini to extract type, severity, location, population and a short message into a 24-byte code and to rebuild a readable alert on the receive side. Offline emergency communication is the most obvious 'why on-device' story, so expect many similar entries among 3,200 participants (AeroMesh AI, HARBOR, ReliefCopilot, Last Message and BLE-mesh-plus-AI builds already exist).

There are SDK traps on iOS. Firebase docs say on-device function calling is supported but give no code example, and structured-output docs are 'coming soon'. The reliable path (native FoundationModels @Generable) bypasses Firebase AI Logic and would break the hackathon requirement. Getting a ~3B model in a multi-turn session to reliably choose between asking a follow-up and calling packMessage is unproven. Foundation Models in the Simulator needs Apple Intelligence enabled on the host Mac. With 8 GB RAM, running Xcode, the Simulator, the system model and Chrome together will swap heavily. Chrome Nano on an 8 GB M1 likely fails the 16 GB CPU path, and the GPU path is unverified.
red.existing_competitors:
Direct or near-direct prior art:
- EchoSign (github.com/TruVortex/echosign, CXC 2026 hackathon). Gemini packs a roughly 200-word report into a 24-byte structured code (type, severity, lat/long, population, 8-character message, CRC) and rebuilds a readable alert on the receive side. It is the same 'semantic codec' idea, done in the cloud.
- Other hackathon builds in offline emergency messaging: AeroMesh AI (compresses an offline SOS queue and forwards it by SMS to a command dashboard), HARBOR (mesh to AI structured incident reports), ReliefCopilot (offline SMS/PA messages), Last Message (local-first Gemma emergency app), and a BLE mesh messenger extended with on-device AI.

The receiver and enrichment half already exists:
- inReach SMS Bridge relays inReach texts to any webhook, with AI and weather bots as the stated use case.
- Backpacking Light 'Uplink' provides environmental intelligence and forecasts for satellite messengers.
- Garmin inReach Weather, the 'wxnow' email-forecast trick, and the reported 1-800-ChatGPT-over-inReach workaround.
- Bridge AI (iOS) turns long emails into short SMS summaries and expands short SMS replies into full emails. That is the same compress/expand pattern as the reply path, without satellite.

The shortening half already exists:
- Apple Writing Tools 'Concise' and 'Summary', on-device on all Apple Intelligence iPhones.
- Short Text (iOS abbreviation shortener with a target length) and SmartSMS AI Shorten.
- Garmin, ZOLEO and Bivy preset check-ins and quick texts with GPS.
- Apple's own Emergency SOS compression and questionnaire.

Platforms making the problem smaller:
- Garmin inReach Messenger Plus: 1,600 characters, photos, voice.
- ZOLEO: 900 characters.
- T-Satellite / Starlink Direct-to-Cell: app data for WhatsApp, Maps and AccuWeather on 60+ phones, with Starlink V2 expected in 2027.

Research: LLM semantic compression for bandwidth-limited UAV links (arXiv 2508.12043) and the meshcompress benchmark on Meshtastic payloads.

No shipped product combines all three parts: on-device schema packing on the sender, cloud enrichment on the receiver, and cloud reply compression to a shared codebook. The combination is novel, but each piece has precedent.
red.mitigations:
Treat this as 'risky but salvageable'. Its strongest asset is real: the sender is offline by definition, so on-device is required by physics rather than chosen as a preference. Build the pitch around that asymmetry, not around byte savings.

1. Reframe the audience. Lead with groups whose limits are hard and lasting: the installed base of inReach Mini/Mini 2 users (about 154 usable chars), plain satellite SMS from Apple/Skylo/Starlink, Meshtastic (about 200 bytes), and expedition bases and SAR teams. Drop the internet-shutdown framing or move it to future work. If it stays, add optional pre-shared-key encryption and be honest about the byte cost.

2. Make each platform truly hybrid.
- Web receiver: decode incoming frames instantly with PREFER_ON_DEVICE (fast and private, with a deterministic parser as backstop). Use cloud for enrichment, translation and reply compression, and show inferenceSource badges.
- iOS sender: when any link exists (weak cell, Starlink data), use cloud for richer packing, for example Maps grounding to name the nearest landmark. When offline, use only on-device. The audience should see the router switch live.
- Cut the Chrome laptop sender, or keep it only as a fallback to the deterministic form.

3. Replace search-grounded weather with cloud function calling to a real global forecast API such as Open-Meteo, and use Maps grounding for huts and ranger stations. Show sources and timestamps. Phrase everything as information, never as orders ('descend now' goes).

4. Prove the AI earns its place. Build a 50-message eval set of rambling texts and dictation. Report critical-fact recall, round-trip fidelity and median characters for three approaches: the on-device LLM, Apple Writing Tools Concise, and a plain form. Put those numbers in the video.

5. Stay on Firebase AI Logic for every on-device call. Do not bypass it with native @Generable. On day 1, spike HybridModel plus a tool call in the Simulator, with Apple Intelligence enabled on this macOS 26.6 / Xcode 27.2 host. If tool calling is flaky, fall back to single-turn output in a strict line format, parsed deterministically. Also check Chrome Nano on day 1 (chrome://on-device-internals) and drop any web on-device sender claim if it isn't available.

6. Stage the demo honestly. Label the transport 'satellite SMS (simulated)'. Ingest frames by paste or QR, or through an inbound-only path. inReach can message an email address, so an inbound email parse to a Cloud Function avoids SMS registration. Inbound Twilio is fine; avoid outbound US SMS that needs A2P 10DLC. Record the real send on a physical iPhone if the user has one.

7. Plan the scope. Days 1-2: spikes and codec spec. Days 3-6: iOS sender. Days 6-8: web receiver. Day 9: Remote Config codebook, App Check and Auth. Day 10: eval. Day 11: video. Cut the share extension, Android and the Twilio replies first.

demo.storyboard:
Opening line: "When every character costs 15 seconds, what do you say?" Throughout, an ON-DEVICE or IN-CLOUD badge stays on screen with a little latency counter, so the hybrid split is visible in every shot.

BEAT 1 (0:00-0:20) Hook. A black screen shows a phone status bar going from LTE to "SOS / Satellite". Three facts appear as captions, each with its source: satellite texts take at least 15 s (Apple), inReach allows 160 characters, and there were 313 internet shutdowns in 52 countries in 2025 (Access Now). Voice-over: "Millions of people can now text from places with no internet. But they can only send a few words, slowly." Use only the cited stats and skip stock footage, which saves time and avoids rights problems.

BEAT 2 (0:20-0:55) Offline sender, the hero shot. The Mac's Wi-Fi is visibly OFF in the menu bar. The iPhone Simulator shows a "Satellite only - 160 chars" banner. A 480-character message is dictated and shown sped up: "ok so we're behind schedule, Sam rolled his ankle, there's 3 of us, low on water, phone at 40%..." The user taps Telegraph. The on-device Foundation Models session asks one thing: "Where are you heading, and when?" The user answers "Refugio Frey, ~18:00". The byte meter drops from red 480 to green 131 with an ON-DEVICE badge. Fact chips tick off: 3 people, 1 injured (ankle), water, ETA 18:00, battery 40%, Plus Code. A "They will read:" panel shows the device decoding its own frame back into prose.

BEAT 3 (0:55-1:10) The frame travels. Share sheet goes to Messages, with satellite labeled as the target link. On screen: "OK P3 INJ1:ankle NEED:water ETA1800 >RefFrey BAT40 @...+..". One beat makes the point that the frame is still readable in a plain SMS app, so a receiver without the app can read it. The frame then lands on the web dashboard, either through a Twilio inbound number or, more honestly, a labeled "simulated satellite link" that enforces 160 chars and a 15 s delay.

BEAT 4 (1:10-1:45) Connected receiver, cloud enrichment. An IN-CLOUD badge shows. The briefing card has a map pin from the Plus Code, the people, injury, needs and ETA, and the battery level. Real numbers come from a cloud weather tool call: "Gusts 65 km/h from ~16:00 at this point. Sunset 20:41. ETA is after the wind arrives." Under that: suggested questions to ask back. The "aha" is a language toggle: the same frame shows as a Spanish briefing for Mom and an English one for the rescue coordinator. "The frame is language-neutral."

BEAT 5 (1:45-2:15) The hard half: reply compression. Mom types a 700-character anxious reply. The cloud squeezes it into a 152-character codebook frame and shows a diff: emotion trimmed, all 4 instructions kept. She sends it by SMS. Back on the offline phone (Wi-Fi still off), the frame is pasted or shared in. On-device, it expands into a 4-step checklist: descend by the west trail now, splint the ankle, refill at the stream, check in at 17:00. ON-DEVICE badge.

BEAT 6 (2:15-2:40) Everywhere, on any device. Chrome PWA at the hosted URL: on a machine with Gemini Nano it shows an ON-DEVICE badge, and when Nano isn't there it falls back to cloud with an IN-CLOUD badge. Wi-Fi off with no Nano drops to deterministic form packing, so the app never breaks. A quick Android shot shows the cloud path. Quick context cards: a sailor on inReach, a Starlink direct-to-cell texter, a family during a shutdown. A permanent "Emergency? Use SOS" banner routes to official SOS.

BEAT 7 (2:40-3:00) How it works, then the close. A 10-second diagram: the model sits on-device where the network isn't (sender) and in the cloud where it is (receiver). The Remote Config codebook is cached at both ends, Firestore threads persist offline, and App Check is on. End card: "Telegraph. Say more with less." Hosted URL plus "Try Judge Mode: two tabs, one simulated satellite link."
demo.weak_spots:
1) The grounded storm line could be a made-up forecast on camera. Google Search grounding won't give a forecast for an exact point. Get the forecast and sunset times from a weather API through a cloud function call (Open-Meteo is free, global and needs no key), and let Gemini only phrase the result. Keep Search grounding for ferry and road status only.

2) Showing "offline" honestly. The iOS Simulator has no airplane mode and shares the Mac's network. Turn the Mac's Wi-Fi off on camera for the sender shots and record the receiver on a second device, or record the two halves separately and composite them. Also, App Attest does not work in the Simulator, so App Check needs the debug provider there. Say that in the README.

3) Judge tryability depends on how the web sender is set up. The plan says ONLY_ON_DEVICE for web packing, but most judges won't have Nano, and Nano on an 8 GB M1 is unverified. Use PREFER_ON_DEVICE (packs in the cloud when online, badge visible) plus a Judge Mode: prefilled rambling message, two-tab pairing, and a simulated 160-char / 15 s link. Without that, judges get a form and conclude the AI isn't needed. iOS will effectively be video-only for judges, since TestFlight needs a device with Apple Intelligence.

4) "Why not just type less, or use a form?" The deterministic fallback invites this question. Make the AI's value visible: messy dictation under stress, the follow-up question for missing fields, another language on the receiving end, and above all reply compression plus offline expansion. Show the fact-diff so lossy compression looks safe, not risky.

5) Apple and Garmin already partly cover this. Apple compresses SOS messages and Garmin has preset messages. Lead with the two-way loop, receiver enrichment and the language-neutral frame, not byte savings.

6) The shutdown use case is ethically delicate. SMS during a shutdown is plaintext and easy to monitor, so sending structured locations could put users at risk. Keep it as a secondary audience, offer a mode that leaves location out, and lead with outdoor and maritime users, which are cleaner and more visual.

7) Adoption friction. Both ends benefit from the app. That is reduced by frames a person can read without the app and a receiver dashboard that opens from a link with nothing to install. Show both explicitly.

8) Scope for 11 days solo. iOS on-device multi-turn plus tool calls, a web sender and receiver, a weather tool, Firestore threads and Remote Config is already full. Cut Twilio unless days are left over, skip the Chrome extension, and keep Android cloud-only.

9) The 3B on-device model will sometimes miss tool calls or drop fields. A deterministic validator plus the round-trip check has to catch every miss, or the demo can fail live. Pre-test the exact demo script 20 or more times.

10) The receiver side is cloud-only, so the hybrid story rests on the sender. State the split clearly as on-device where the network isn't, cloud where it is, so judges read it as a deliberate design choice rather than a thin use of hybrid.

finalist.name: Blindfill: the cloud reads the form, only your device reads you
finalist.merged_from: Blindfill (privacy-split lens) + Formbridge (chrome-native lens). These were near-duplicates. The merged version takes from Formbridge: answering in your own language with output in the form's language and format, Chrome's on-device Translator API as a bridge for languages Nano doesn't support, the side panel for HTML forms, and the iOS loop for reading paper letters. From Fieldwise/Kappa it borrows the 'two independent readers' check: the model's passport extraction is cross-checked against a deterministic MRZ parser and checksum.
finalist.pitch:
USER: Anyone filling high-stakes official forms in a language or legal register that isn't their own. That includes about 304M international migrants (UN DESA 2024), international students, visa applicants (11.7M Schengen short-stay applications in 2024), refugees, benefits and tax filers, and the NGO caseworkers who help them. A Brazilian in Japan, an Indian in Canada and a Syrian in Germany face the same problem.

PROBLEM: Forms are long, full of jargon and unforgiving: date order, surname order, terms like 'Geburtsname'. Mistakes lead to refusals, lost fees and delays (about 1.7M Schengen refusals in 2024). Today's AI shortcuts (ChatGPT, Instafill, form-filling extensions, Chrome's cloud-backed Gemini fill experiments) need you to upload your passport, address, income and family details, which together make an identity-theft kit. Migrants and asylum seekers have the most to lose. The insight: understanding a form is public knowledge; only the answers are private.

ON-DEVICE JOB (ONLY_ON_DEVICE for anything that touches the user's values): (1) Vault: extracts an identity profile from photos of a passport, ID, permits and payslips. On Chrome this uses the Prompt API with image input and a JSON schema; on iOS, Vision OCR followed by Foundation Models with tool-call output. A deterministic ICAO MRZ parser and checksum act as a second, independent reader. The vault is encrypted and never synced. (2) Answer in your own language: the user answers each field in their language, and the device writes it in the form's language and local format (DD.MM.YYYY, surname first, transliteration, postcode). Chrome's on-device Translator API wraps Nano for languages outside Nano's set. (3) Fills fields locally and drafts short free-text answers such as 'purpose of journey' (under 256 tokens). (4) Private consistency checks, for example 'Your passport expires 6 weeks after return; consulates require 3 months' or 'Birth name differs from current name'. (5) Sensitivity router: an on-device enum labels each help question as about_the_form or about_me, and about_me questions never leave the device.

CLOUD JOB (ONLY_IN_CLOUD; every input is a blank public document): Gemini reads the blank form PDF and its 10-40 pages of guidance notes (PDF input and long context are cloud-only). It emits a 'form card': for each field, a canonical profile key, a plain-language explanation, format rules, conditional logic, required documents and common reasons for rejection. Google Search grounding keeps it to current official guidance, and the card is translated into 100+ languages. Cards are cached in a public Firestore library keyed by form fingerprint, so the next person anywhere filling the same form makes zero LLM calls. Firestore rules reject any document that contains personal-field keys.

DEMO MOMENT: Split screen with a live 'Cloud Ledger' that logs every byte sent to Gemini: 'schengen-application.pdf (blank, public): 0 personal fields'. A synthetic specimen passport is photographed and an ON_DEVICE badge pulses as the vault fills. Wi-Fi goes off and the presenter taps Fill: about 37 fields across a 9-page form fill in seconds. 'Purpose of journey' is drafted locally from a one-line note typed in Portuguese, and a red flag appears for passport expiry. The UI switches to Arabic and every explanation appears from the cached card. On the iPhone, the letter that arrives later is photographed, its deadline is extracted on-device, and a tool call adds it to the calendar. Closing line: 'Gemini read the form. Only this phone read the passport.'

PLATFORMS: A web PWA on Firebase Hosting for PDF forms (pdf-lib), plus a Chrome extension side panel for HTML forms that sends only field labels to the cloud and fills values locally (the Best Web/Chrome angle). An iOS SwiftUI app with HybridModel: vault from photos, form review, letter reader. Android is cloud-path only and not needed.

FIREBASE: AI Logic hybrid inference (ONLY_ON_DEVICE for the vault, fill and checks; ONLY_IN_CLOUD for form understanding with PDF input and Search grounding). Firestore as the public form-card library, with rules that enforce privacy. Cloud Storage for blank PDFs. App Check (reCAPTCHA Enterprise on web, App Attest on iOS; a custom provider or hosted iframe for the extension). Remote Config (model names, inference mode per task, prompt versions, per-country format rules). Anonymous Auth. Hosting.

KEY RISKS AND SCOPE: (1) Lock in 3 verified fillable AcroForm PDFs plus 1 HTML form on day 1; XFA forms, such as some Canadian IMM forms, are out. (2) Nano on the 8 GB M1 is unverified. The MRZ parser plus the cloud's canonical keys can fill most fields with no on-device AI, iOS carries the on-device showcase, and judges without Nano get a synthetic 'demo persona' clearly bannered as cloud. (3) Metadata leak: fetching the asylum form's card reveals intent, so download the whole catalog instead. (4) A mandatory review screen and no auto-submit. (5) Differentiate from Chrome's own autofill on PDFs, explanations in your language, conditional logic and consistency checks.
finalist.why_finalist: Rank 3. It has the cleanest and most principled split by data class in the pool. Public meaning goes to the cloud once and is shared worldwide; private values never leave the device. The shared Firestore library pushes cloud cost per user toward zero, a hybrid design judges can understand from one diagram. It uses genuinely cloud-only capabilities (PDF input, long context, grounding, 100+ languages) for the right reason. The global audience is huge and specific, with measurable pain (refusals, lost fees). Merging in Formbridge adds the answer-in-your-own-language flow and the iOS letter loop, so both platforms have a real job. Main caution: Google's own Chrome autofill experiments overlap, so the pitch should lead with PDFs, explanations in your language and the Cloud Ledger.

judge.rationale:
I've seen about 300 submissions this week, and this one would land in roughly my top 5%. Its central idea is the strongest framing of hybrid inference I've seen: the job is split by whether the data is public or private, not by what each model can do. "The form is public knowledge, the answers are private" is easy to grasp and hard to dispute. It explains why each half runs where it does. The cloud gets PDF input, long context and Search grounding because it only ever sees blank public documents. The device does the image-to-JSON vault, translation and local fill. Almost every other entry uses hybrid as "on-device if available, otherwise cloud," so this stands out.

The shared form-card library in Firestore is a smart move. One cloud call per form, worldwide, then zero calls for every later user. Firestore rules that reject personal-field keys are a privacy promise the platform actually enforces, which a judge can check.

TECH (8): The project uses the SDK in depth: Prompt API image input with a JSON schema, the Translator API, PDF input plus grounding in the cloud, iOS HybridModel with tool calls, App Check, Remote Config and Firestore rules. Using a deterministic ICAO MRZ checksum as a second, independent reader is the kind of engineering judgment judges reward. It loses points because nearly everything is set to ONLY_ON_DEVICE or ONLY_IN_CLOUD. The SDK's main feature, automatic fallback, is barely used, so a strict judge could see "two pipelines glued together" rather than hybrid inference.

DESIGN (8): If executed well, this is a full product. It has a vault, field explanations in your language, consistency flags, a mandatory review screen and no auto-submit. The Cloud Ledger is a memorable visual that carries the whole pitch. The risk is fragmentation across three surfaces: the PWA, the Chrome extension and iOS.

IMPACT (8): The audience is global, specific and sized (304M migrants, Schengen refusal numbers), and the demo solves the problem live. It doesn't reach 9 for three reasons:
- There is no evidence from real users, such as a quote from an NGO caseworker.
- Many visa applications have moved to online portals, so the PDF path is less relevant than the pitch suggests.
- Wrong legal guidance in a form card, such as an incorrect passport-validity rule, could cause the very refusals the app is meant to prevent.

IDEA (8.5): It is truly non-obvious and shows understanding of the problem, especially the metadata leak (fetching only the asylum form's card reveals intent) and the "download the whole catalog" fix. It isn't a 9 because it sits next to two known categories, PII redaction and AI form-fill (Instafill, and Chrome's own Gemini autofill). Google judges will know Chrome's AI autofill well and will expect a sharp answer to "how is this different from Chrome's own autofill?"
judge.biggest_weakness: The headline privacy half, the vault and the fill, is ONLY_ON_DEVICE. Most judges, and possibly the builder's 8 GB M1, won't have Gemini Nano, so the hosted app falls back to a "demo persona" bannered as cloud. That means judges are asked to believe the core promise rather than experience it. At the same time, the SDK's actual hybrid fallback is barely used, so the "how effectively it uses hybrid inference" criterion is open to a "two separate pipelines" critique. Scope sprawl makes this worse: PWA, Chrome extension, iOS app and a letter reader in 11 days, solo, could leave every surface thin.
judge.best_upgrade:
Turn the Cloud Ledger from a log into an enforced egress firewall with an explicit routing policy, set in Remote Config, that maps each data sensitivity class to an inference mode:
- Public tasks (field explanations, "about_the_form" help questions, translating the form card) use PREFER_ON_DEVICE with real cloud fallback. This shows the SDK's hybrid behavior legitimately.
- Private tasks (the vault, filling, drafting answers, consistency checks) follow "Nano, then deterministic (MRZ parser plus the card's canonical keys), never the cloud."
- Every outbound cloud payload passes through one gate that checks it against the vault's values, with fuzzy matching. The gate blocks and visibly flags any leak, and the demo includes a deliberate leak attempt that gets caught.

A judge without Nano then still sees privacy that is provable and enforced, plus visible hybrid switching. Pair this with cutting scope to the Chrome extension side panel (real portals, the Best Web/Chrome angle) plus iOS, and drop the PWA PDF path and the letter reader.

fatal_flaws: The on-device AI is mostly decorative. MRZ parsing, date and surname reordering, field filling and the passport-expiry flag are all deterministic code. The hero demo moment ('37 fields fill in seconds with Wi-Fi off') is rule-based autofill, not Gemini Nano: one Nano call takes seconds on an M1, so per-field AI could not run 'in seconds'. The only heavy LLM work is a one-time cloud batch job that is cached, so the cloud is barely called live either. Judges scoring 'how effectively it uses hybrid inference' could conclude that neither model does much in the demo.

It never uses the SDK's defining feature, cloud fallback. Every task is pinned to ONLY_ON_DEVICE or ONLY_IN_CLOUD, which is two models behind a hand-written router rather than hybrid inference. On judges' machines without Nano, the private path cannot run at all, so they see a synthetic 'demo persona' bannered as cloud and never experience the core claim. On iOS, HybridModel(primary: SystemLanguageModel, secondary: Gemini) falls back to the cloud automatically. Unless the vault and letter tasks bypass HybridModel and call FoundationModels directly, OCR'd passport text could leak to Gemini, which breaks the pitch's central promise. I could not confirm whether iOS HybridModel has an on-device-only mode because the shared web-search budget ran out.

The 'answer in your own language' promise breaks for the personas in the pitch. The Prompt API accepts only en/ja/es (de/fr added per May 2026 localized docs), so Portuguese and Arabic answers need Chrome's separate Translator API, which is not Firebase AI Logic. On this Mac, Apple Foundation Models reports da, de, en, es, fr, it, ja, ko, nb, nl, pt, sv, tr, vi and zh, with no Arabic, so the 'Syrian in Germany' persona cannot run on-device in Arabic on iOS.

The real target-form population is shrinking or out of scope. USCIS forms are widely reported as dynamic XFA (they show a 'Please wait...' page in Chrome), Canada's IMM forms are XFA, and many Schengen states use online portals (France-Visas, Germany's VIDEX), with the EU VAP platform expected around 2028. Fillable AcroForm immigration PDFs are a minority. That pushes the real value onto the Chrome extension for HTML portals, the most fragile surface: dynamic multi-step forms, session timeouts, and App Check in MV3 where reCAPTCHA cannot load, so a custom provider is needed.

It collides with the sponsor's own product. Since November 2025 Chrome's enhanced autofill fills passport, driver's license and ID fields, and 'Find and fill with Gemini' rolled out in the US on Oct 28 2026. Google judges will ask how this differs from Chrome autofill, and the pitch casts Google's own Gemini fill feature as the privacy villain. iOS 26's Preview app also offers AutoFill for PDF forms.

The public form-card library can be poisoned. If clients generate and write cards to Firestore, any anonymous user can plant wrong guidance for a high-stakes legal form that everyone else then trusts. Firestore rules that reject 'personal-field keys' check key names, not values, so they are privacy theater. Cards must be written only by a Cloud Function (Blaze plan) and carry a human-verified flag.

The scope does not fit the time. A web PWA (pdf-lib, an on-device vault, a browser MRZ OCR model, the Translator API, a service worker), an MV3 Chrome extension (Firebase bundling, a custom App Check provider, HTML field mapping), a SwiftUI iOS app (Vision OCR, Keychain vault, EventKit tool calls, an App Check debug provider in the Simulator) and a grounded card pipeline add up to roughly 14-16 agent-days of work against 11 days available, before the video and write-up.

The card pipeline carries correctness and legal risk. Gemini-generated 'common rejection reasons' and conditional logic on visa forms can be hallucinated, and wrong advice here is costly. Developer forum reports say Search grounding combined with structured JSON output returns empty grounding metadata or drops text on Gemini 3.x, so it needs two calls. In the US, field-by-field advice on immigration forms comes close to unauthorized-practice rules (8 CFR 292), so the impact story needs careful disclaimers.
red.existing_competitors:
On-device Gemini Nano form fillers are already a well-worn category. Form Genie (Devpost) fills web forms with Nano through the Prompt API. PrIDA (Devpost) fills forms locally from a stored profile. Fillo, a Chrome Built-in AI Challenge 2025 entry, maps résumé data to job application forms using Nano. Donbrico Autofill AI (Chrome Web Store) runs Nano locally with an optional bring-your-own cloud key. Forma (Product Hunt) claims a zero-cloud design on Nano, and Nanofill fills fields with dummy data. Formbuddy says documents never leave the device and lists visa and passport applications among its uses.

Visa and passport autofill extensions also exist. Indian Visa Autofill Pro parses passports locally and fills the Indian visa portal. Migrawise Autofill targets Canada's IRCC portal for consultants. VisaField, Intellivisa, VisaTrove Filler and AutoFill Copilot ('Fill Tax, Visa & Government Forms') round out the group.

Cloud AI PDF fillers: Instafill.ai has USCIS, visa and passport form categories, a Chrome extension, converts flat PDFs to fillable ones, and has you upload documents. SimplePDF hosts I-485 and similar forms.

Immigrant form explainers:
- ImmiGuide (iOS/iPad/Mac App Store) is close to the iOS half of this idea: field-by-field USCIS explanations in 8 languages including Arabic, plus passport or ID scan to pre-fill.
- JustiGuide (TechCrunch, Nov 2025) offers an AI assistant in 12 languages and reports 47k users.
- Filevine ImmigrationAI serves lawyers with questionnaires in 170 languages.
- Hackathon projects include Formigrant (Devpost: multilingual immigration form assistant with PDF upload, a Gemini breakdown and voice Q&A), FormFriend (photograph any official form and have it translated), Fillify (lablab, USCIS form filling), NavigateHome AI, formi and immigr-aid.

Platform features from the sponsor:
- Chrome enhanced autofill has filled passport, driver's license and vehicle data since November 2025.
- 'Find and fill with Gemini' launched in the US on Oct 28 2026.
- iOS 26's Preview app offers AutoFill for PDF forms.

Previous Firebase/Chrome hybrid winners from the Built-in AI Challenge 2025 were Mentelo (a voice tech-support extension) and Trail (an offline trail companion); no form filler won. The idea's novel twist is real: the form is public, the answers are private, plus a shared library of form cards. But each half of it (private form filling, and explaining forms to immigrants in their language) has many prior entries.
red.mitigations:
1. Give the on-device LLM work that rules cannot do:
- Read non-MRZ documents into the vault (residence permit, payslip, bank statement, utility bill) using Nano image input and a JSON schema.
- Have it decide which conditional sections of the form apply, given the vault.
- Run cross-document consistency checks: a transliteration variant of a name, a name on a payslip that differs from the passport, an address that differs from the permit.
- Keep MRZ, date and order formatting deterministic, and say so openly ('rules where rules suffice, Nano where judgment is needed'). Show real per-call ON_DEVICE timings rather than a pulsing badge.

2. Use real fallback deliberately and make the router the hero. Questions about the form, re-phrasing explanations and card lookups run PREFER_ON_DEVICE and fall back to cloud, which is safe because the data is public. Questions about the user stay ONLY_ON_DEVICE. In the demo, show the same SDK call landing ON_DEVICE or IN_CLOUD depending on the sensitivity label, so fallback reads as a privacy policy rather than something avoided.

3. On iOS, call FoundationModels directly for private tasks. Its native @Generable guided generation gives real structured output with no tool-call hack, and no silent cloud fallback. Use HybridModel only for public tasks, and verify on day 1 whether it can be forced on-device.

4. Day-1 checks. On this Mac, Chrome already has v3Nano weights downloaded (4.0 GB, with a GPU program cache), FoundationModels reports 'available', and an iOS 27 Simulator runtime is installed, so platform risk is lower than assumed. Confirm with a real Prompt API image plus JSON schema call through the Firebase hybrid SDK before committing.

5. Cut to two surfaces: the web PWA and iOS. Drop the MV3 extension, which brings App Check custom-provider work and fragile HTML portals; the PWA can still compete for Best Web. If time remains on day 9, add a minimal extension.

6. Choose forms that are verified AcroForm and genuinely global, for example IRS W-8BEN (used by non-US freelancers and investors worldwide), a fillable Schengen form from a specific consulate, and one residence-registration or university form. Rule out XFA on day 1.
