7. Generate cards only in a Cloud Function, with clients read-only, a version and human-verified flag, and source citations. Use two calls: a grounded search first, then a second call that produces the structured card.

8. Position against Chrome autofill as complementary, not as the villain: 'Autofill knows your passport number; it doesn't know Geburtsname, the 3-month validity rule, or which section applies to you.' Make the villain uploading a passport to a chatbot.

9. Build personas around languages both models support (pt, es, de, fr, ja). Handle Arabic through Chrome's on-device Translator API and Apple's on-device Translation framework, and disclose that this is not AI Logic.

10. For judges without Nano, add a clearly labelled path that runs a synthetic passport through the cloud, plus a side-by-side recording in the video of the real on-device run.

demo.storyboard:
Hero device: split screen for the whole video. App on the left, live CLOUD LEDGER on the right, with a running counter that reads "Personal fields sent to cloud: 0". The counter staying at 0 while sensitive data moves on screen is the visual idea; every beat shows it again.

BEAT 1 - Hook (0:00-0:15)
On screen: a generic, unbranded chatbot box. A passport photo is dragged into it. Freeze frame; red labels appear on the name, DOB, passport number and address: "identity-theft kit".
VO: "304 million people fill official forms in a language that isn't theirs. Today's AI shortcut is to upload your passport."
Cut to the title card: "BLINDFILL - the cloud reads the form. Only your device reads you."

BEAT 2 - The cloud reads the blank form (0:15-0:40)
On screen: drag the blank Schengen harmonised application PDF into the web app. A cold run, never cached, sped up 4x with a timer overlay. The ledger logs "schengen-application.pdf (blank, public) 412 KB -> Gemini [IN_CLOUD]" and "Personal fields: 0". The form card renders: field 21 explained in plain language, conditional logic ("only if minor"), common refusal reasons, and a Search-grounded source link. Then a toast: "Saved to public library. Next person anywhere: 0 LLM calls."
VO: "Understanding a form is public knowledge, so Gemini does that part."

BEAT 3 - The vault fills on-device (0:40-1:05)
On screen: the webcam shows a printed ICAO 'UTOPIA' specimen passport (the official fictitious state; no real country). An ON_DEVICE badge pulses while the vault fields fill in one by one. A second chip reads "MRZ checksum: 2 independent readers agree". The ledger counter does not move.
VO: "Only your answers are private, so they never leave this machine."

BEAT 4 - Offline fill (1:05-1:40)
On screen: click Wi-Fi off in the menu bar (an OFFLINE chip is visible), then tap Fill. Page thumbnails flip as 37 fields fill across 9 pages, with surnames, dates in the form's format and transliteration. The user types in Portuguese, "vou visitar minha irmã em Lyon", and 'Purpose of journey' is drafted in English with an ON_DEVICE badge. A red flag slides in: "Passport valid 6 weeks after return; consulates require 3 months. This is a common refusal reason."
VO: "No network. Seconds. And it caught a mistake that costs people their visa fee."

BEAT 5 - Global and Chrome (1:40-2:05)
On screen: switch the UI language to Arabic; the layout flips right-to-left and the explanations load from the cached card while still offline. Hard cut to the Chrome extension side panel on an HTML form (a demo form, not a real government site). The ledger logs "22 field LABELS -> cloud" and "0 VALUES". Values fill locally.
VO: "Any form, any language, PDF or web page. Only the questions leave."

BEAT 6 - iPhone and the sensitivity router (2:05-2:35)
On screen: the iOS app shows the same vault, with an Apple Foundation Models badge. A synthetic 'Immigration Office' letter is IMPORTED from Photos (the Simulator has no camera). The deadline is extracted on-device, and a tool call adds a calendar event. Two questions are asked:
- "What does 'sponsor' mean here?" is labelled about_the_form and goes to the cloud.
- "Can I still travel if my permit expires in March?" is labelled about_me and stays on the device.
The router chip animates for each one.
VO: "The phone decides what is about the form and what is about you."

BEAT 7 - Receipt and call to action (2:35-3:00)
On screen: an end-of-session receipt: "Cloud calls: 3 | Public bytes: 1.2 MB | Personal fields sent: 0 | On-device calls: 41". A short flash of the DevTools Network tab proves the ledger is real. A strip shows the stack: AI Logic hybrid, App Check, Firestore library, Remote Config, Anonymous Auth, Hosting. The URL appears with "Try it with the Utopia specimen passport. No Nano needed."
VO (closing line): "Gemini read the form. Only this phone read the passport."
demo.weak_spots:
1. Form-filling looks boring on camera, and a judge from Google may read it as just Chrome Autofill or Gemini-in-Chrome fill. Two things carry the video: the Cloud Ledger with its counter stuck at 0, and the red-flag catch. If either feels mocked or slow, the demo falls flat. Build the ledger as a real wrapper around every Firebase AI Logic, Firestore and Storage request, and show the DevTools Network tab for 2 seconds to prove it.

2. There are too many beats for 3 minutes: vault, fill, own-language answer, Arabic, extension, iOS letter, router. Protect the hybrid-split proof (beats 2 to 4) and the iOS router, which is the most non-obvious hybrid idea and supports the multi-platform Grand Prize case. The extension can be a 10-second cameo, and the letter reader can be cut if time runs short. Do not add anything else.

3. Offline is a hard technical bet. ONLY_ON_DEVICE with Wi-Fi off needs four things, and each one must be tested on day 1, not day 10:
   - Nano is already downloaded.
   - A service worker caches the PWA.
   - Firestore offline persistence holds the cards.
   - The Firebase SDK or App Check does not fail when it cannot refresh a token offline.

4. Nano on the 8 GB M1 is unverified. The Prompt API needs about 22 GB of free disk, and there are reports of hardware-requirement errors even on newer Macs. Image input to Nano is also less mature, and it may misread small passport text. Make the MRZ parser the primary reader and Nano only a cross-check, and never show a raw Nano extraction on camera without rehearsing it. If Chrome Nano will not run, film the offline beat on the iOS Simulator (Mac Wi-Fi off covers both).

5. The iOS Simulator has no camera. Every "photograph" step on iOS must be shown as a photo import, or filmed on a real iPhone if the user has one. Apple Foundation Models in the Simulator needs Apple Intelligence enabled on macOS.

6. Tryability gap for judges. By design, personal-value AI runs ONLY_ON_DEVICE, so a judge without Nano gets the cloud 'demo persona' path, and that weakens the privacy story at the moment they try it. The hosted app needs:
   - a one-click "Utopia specimen kit" (passport image plus persona);
   - deterministic MRZ parsing and deterministic rules for the consistency checks, so the core loop works without any LLM;
   - 3 curated forms that always work;
   - "bring your own blank PDF" behind a beta label, because XFA or non-fillable PDFs will fail on a judge's first try;
   - a clear "on-device vs. cloud in your browser" capability panel.

   iOS and the extension will mostly be judged from video. Ship a TestFlight build or a packed extension anyway.

7. Credibility and legal hygiene:
   - Use only ICAO specimen data, with no real state seals.
   - Show no real chatbot brands in the hook.
   - Do not present the app as official.
   - Put a "not legal advice / you review before submitting" notice on the review screen.
   - Cite the stats on screen: 304M migrants (UN DESA 2024); 11.7M Schengen applications and about 1.7M refusals at about 14.8% (European Commission, May 2025).

8. The impact case would be stronger with one real voice: a 5-second quote from an NGO caseworker or international-student office.
   The growth story is currently implied. Say it outright:
   - Caseworkers and university international offices are the distribution channel.
   - The public form-card library has a network effect.
   - Each card can be a public, indexable page ("Schengen form field 21 explained in Arabic") that brings people in.

9. Metadata leakage. Downloading the whole card catalog has to work offline too. Otherwise the Arabic beat could make a network call that reveals which form the user cares about.

10. Name risk: "Blindfill" could be read as an accessibility app for blind users. Fix it with the tagline in the first 10 seconds.

finalist.name: Denominator: adds the missing baseline to every statistic you read
finalist.pitch:
USER: Anyone who reads numbers about finance, crime, politics or health online (about 6B internet users). The core audience is the roughly 25% of adults in OECD countries at or below Level 1 numeracy (OECD Survey of Adult Skills 2023), plus students, journalists and statistics teachers. It works on any site and in any language that the on-device and cloud models support.

PROBLEM: Relative numbers with no baseline ('50% higher risk', 'crime doubled', 'fund returned 300%') drive real decisions. The classic case is the 1995 UK pill scare: 'doubles thrombosis risk', in absolute terms 1 in 7,000 rising to 2 in 7,000, is estimated to have caused about 13,000 extra abortions the following year (Gigerenzer et al.). I found no extension that converts relative numbers to absolute ones while you read; the closest is RealRisk, a manual calculator.

ON-DEVICE JOB: Runs on every page view in the Chrome extension and on every article shared into the iOS reader. A regex pre-filter keeps only sentences with numbers or ratio words. The on-device model turns each claim into a typed record: {kind: relative_change | absolute | percent_of_what | per_capita_missing | cumulative_vs_annual, value, outcome, population, timeframe, baseline_on_page}. On web this uses JSON-schema output; on iOS, Foundation Models with a recordClaim(...) tool call, in chunks under 4,096 tokens. Deterministic code, never the LLM, does all the arithmetic: absolute risk, extra cases per 100, number needed to treat, per-capita and inflation adjustment. If the baseline is already on the page, no cloud call is made. WHY ON-DEVICE: 10-50 numeric sentences per page across 30-60 pages a day is hundreds of calls per user per day. Reading history about money, health and politics is sensitive. And the underlines have to appear while the page renders.

CLOUD JOB: Runs only when the user taps a claim marked 'baseline missing' (about 1-3 taps a day). Gemini with Google Search grounding finds the reference rate for the right population and timeframe and returns {baseline, population, timeframe, source_url}. The same deterministic math then produces the absolute version. Optionally, it reads the linked study PDF (cloud-only) and checks the headline against the paper's own absolute numbers. Results are cached in Firestore by claim fingerprint, so the next reader of the same headline costs nothing.

DEMO MOMENT: A realistic headline reads 'Daily X linked to 50% higher risk of Y'. A dotted underline appears instantly with an ON-DEVICE badge and keeps working in airplane mode. Hovering shows 'Relative number. Baseline missing.' Tapping 'Find the denominator' shows an IN-CLOUD badge, then a grid of 100 person icons animates: '4 in 100 -> 6 in 100: 2 extra people per 100 (source)'. Cut to the 1995 headline turning into '1 extra case per 7,000 women', with the 13,000 caption. Finish on iPhone through the Safari share sheet with a finance example ('fund returned 300%': over what period, compared with what?) and a crime-statistics example.

PLATFORMS: Chrome extension (main web surface). A hosted web app where you paste a URL or text, so judges can try it without installing anything. An iOS app with a Share extension and reader view, running Foundation Models on-device. Android is optional and cloud-only.

FIREBASE: AI Logic hybrid inference (a PREFER_ON_DEVICE extractor plus a separate ONLY_IN_CLOUD model with Search grounding for baselines and PDFs). App Check. Firestore (shared baseline cache plus user 'this conversion is wrong' flags). Remote Config (pre-filter regexes, prompt versions, per-user daily cloud budget, kill switch). Anonymous Auth. Hosting.

KEY RISKS: (1) Nano is probably not eligible on the 8 GB M1. Open the video on iOS, where Foundation Models runs, record the web on-device path on an eligible machine, and cap the cloud fallback with Remote Config. (2) Extraction errors: underline only high-confidence claims and show the extracted fields. (3) A baseline for the wrong population: always show population, timeframe and source, and say 'not found' rather than guess. (4) Deliberately mix finance, crime and politics examples so it doesn't read as a health app. (5) Scope to relative risk, percent change and per-capita first.
finalist.why_finalist: Rank 4. Highly non-obvious and understandable in 10 seconds. The split is principled by frequency and sensitivity: the device extracts on every page, code does the math, and the cloud fetches only the missing fact, with citations. The Firestore cache shows a cost-aware hybrid design. It is grounded in decades of risk-literacy research, relevant everywhere, and avoids the crowded 'AI fact-checker' space by never ruling on truth. It is the cheapest finalist to build well (extension, share extension, small cloud surface). Weakness: the web on-device path depends on Nano, so the iOS path has to carry the offline demo.

judge.rationale:
Of roughly 300 submissions, this is one of the few where the on-device/cloud split comes from the shape of the workload instead of being added on top. Underlining claims on every page is frequent, needs low latency and touches sensitive reading history, so it runs on-device. Looking up a missing baseline happens one to three times a day and needs knowledge plus a cited source, so it goes to the cloud. Each Firebase piece has a real job: the Firestore claim-fingerprint cache makes the cloud cost shrink as more people use it, Remote Config holds the daily budget and kill switch, App Check and Anonymous Auth gate access. All arithmetic is deterministic code, which is the right call because a judge will check the numbers by hand. Using a recordClaim tool call on iOS to stand in for structured output (which iOS on-device models don't support yet) shows the builder has read the platform limits.

TECH 8: The hybrid usage is strong. It isn't a 9 because the web on-device path may not run on the builder's 8 GB M1, and nearly every judge will hit the cloud fallback path. So the on-device advantage is mostly shown on video rather than something judges experience themselves. Nano will also struggle to tell apart the six claim types, especially percent_of_what versus cumulative_vs_annual. Search grounding also comes with attribution display requirements that cost UI work.

DESIGN 7: The 100-person icon grid is the standard way risk researchers communicate risk, and it gives the demo a memorable visual. The ON-DEVICE and IN-CLOUD badges make the hybrid design visible to the viewer. Having a Chrome extension, a paste-a-link hosted app and an iOS share-sheet reader makes it a real product rather than a proof of concept. It isn't higher because underlining claims on arbitrary news sites (paywalls, ads that load late, hydration) is fragile. The hosted paste-a-link page is also a weaker way to experience it than the extension, and that is the version judges will actually try.

IMPACT 6: The problem is real and the 1995 pill scare is a strong, sourced example. But "6 billion internet users" is not a specific audience. The people who most need this, adults with low numeracy, are the least likely to install a statistics extension. The finance ('300% over what period?') and crime examples are weaker fits than relative risk, so the clearest cases still come from health reporting. Judges will ask who installs this on day one, and the pitch has no good answer.

IDEA 8: It's non-obvious, sits outside every crowded category, and is grounded in established research on how people misread risk (Gigerenzer's work). It also isn't a 'fake news detector': it adds missing context rather than ruling on what's true, which is more defensible. It isn't a 9 because it still belongs to the familiar 'media literacy extension' genre, and fact-check overlays are a common hackathon idea.
judge.biggest_weakness: The audience is too broad and unlikely to install it. 'Everyone who reads statistics' gives judges no specific user, and the low-numeracy readers it is meant to help are the least likely to install a reading-aid extension. On top of that, the product's credibility rests on its least reliable step: finding a baseline for the right population and timeframe through Gemini plus Search. A single confident wrong figure, for example the wrong age group or annual versus lifetime risk, from a judge testing an article of their own would turn a tool against misleading numbers into a source of them. And because the clearest examples come from health news, it will still read as a health app however many finance and crime examples are added.
judge.best_upgrade: Add a Write mode for people who publish numbers, and lead the pitch with it: journalists, science and comms writers, analysts, students and stats teachers. It would check drafts as they are typed, in any editable text area or CMS editor (WordPress, Substack, Medium, Ghost) and in the hosted app's editor. Skip Google Docs, because it draws text on a canvas the extension can't easily read. A bare relative number would get flagged, with a suggested fix ('add the baseline: 4 to 6 in 100') and a cited source. This gives a specific audience that can actually be reached (newsrooms, university writing centres, stats classes), and one fix by a writer reaches thousands of readers. It also adds a stronger reason to stay on-device: embargoed, unpublished drafts can't leave the machine. And the demo gets a tighter story, the 1995 headline caught before it was published. Keep Read mode as the consumer side, and back both modes with a curated base-rate library in Firestore (official statistics, index returns, crime rates per 100k), using grounded search only for gaps. That way the most common baselines come from known tables rather than live search.

fatal_flaws: TERMS OF SERVICE CONFLICT (the most serious problem, and the easiest to miss). The plan keeps a shared Firestore cache of Search-grounded baselines so that 'the next reader of the same headline costs nothing'. That conflicts with the current Gemini API Grounding with Google Search terms (aistudio.google.com/docs/terms). Under those terms you may not 'cache, frame, syndicate, resell' Grounded Results. Grounding is provided 'to the end user who submitted the prompt'. Grounded Results may be shown only together with their Search Suggestions. And without written permission you may not 'modify, or intersperse any other content with' them. The only storage exceptions are display optimisation, the user's own chat history, and temporary reuse in a later prompt. So the cross-user cache, and the cost argument built on it, have to go. Drawing the grounded number straight into an icon grid without the searchEntryPoint chip is also a compliance gray zone. Firebase/Google staff on the jury could notice this.

THE CORE VALUE IS THE PART LEAST LIKELY TO BE CORRECT. Converting a relative number to an absolute one requires (a) the right baseline for the right population and timeframe, and (b) the right effect measure. Search-grounded Gemini will often return a baseline for the wrong population, such as all adults when the study covered women over 50, or a US rate shown to a reader in Germany. Odds ratios and hazard ratios are not risk ratios. RealRisk's own documentation and the iatroX guide warn that multiplying a baseline by any reported relative measure is not valid. A numeracy tool that confidently animates a wrong 'X in 100' grid causes exactly the harm it claims to prevent. Deterministic arithmetic does not help when its inputs are wrong.

THE ON-DEVICE PATH MAY NOT RUN FOR THE BUILDER OR FOR MOST JUDGES. Chrome's Prompt API requires either a GPU with strictly more than 4 GB of VRAM, or 16 GB of RAM with 4+ CPU cores, plus 22 GB of free disk. On the 8 GB M1 this is unverified, and there are forum reports of 'device is not eligible' errors on 8 GB machines and even on an M2 Mac. With PREFER_ON_DEVICE, any user without Nano (Safari, Firefox, mobile Chrome, low-RAM laptops, most judges) silently sends the numeric sentences from every page to the cloud. That turns both the privacy pitch and the 'hundreds of free calls per day' pitch upside down.

'UNDERLINES APPEAR INSTANTLY WHILE THE PAGE RENDERS' IS NOT CREDIBLE. Each claim produces a structured record with 6+ fields, so 10-50 numeric sentences per page means thousands of Nano output tokens. That is likely tens of seconds or more of GPU work per page, and a battery drain on every page view. I could not confirm Nano throughput numbers because the web-search budget ran out, so measure this on day 1. Either way, the demo's 'instant' underline will have to be staged or narrowed to the viewport.

THE 'GLOBAL, ANY LANGUAGE' CLAIM IS OVERSTATED. On-device input and output for Chrome's Prompt API is limited to en, ja, es, de and fr. The task brief says Android is validated only for English and Korean. Grounded baselines will also lean toward English-language and OECD statistics. The project is global in principle and Western-centric in practice.

THE NON-HEALTH EXAMPLES ARE THE WEAKEST ONES, but the user explicitly wants to move away from health. The strongest cases (the 1995 pill scare, '50% higher risk of Y') are health stories. 'Fund returned 300%' is not a missing-denominator problem: the fix is annualisation plus a benchmark, which needs a different kind of claim. 'Crime doubled' needs local per-capita crime counts that Search grounding rarely finds reliably. If the finance and crime segments look weak, the project will read as a health app anyway.

TOO MUCH SCOPE FOR ONE AGENT IN 11 DAYS. The plan includes all of the following. (1) An MV3 extension with content scripts plus an offscreen document for Firebase. (2) App Check in an extension, which has no first-class provider: reCAPTCHA Enterprise needs a registered web domain, and Firebase's own MV3 guidance needs offscreen documents for reCAPTCHA. (3) A hosted web app where pasting a URL needs a server-side fetch proxy to get around CORS. (4) An iOS app plus a Share extension (memory limits, no official way to open the host app, App Attest needs the debug provider on the Simulator). (5) Two tool-schema implementations on iOS: Foundation Models' Tool protocol and Gemini function declarations. (6) Five claim kinds, including inflation and per-capita adjustment, which need global CPI and population data. (7) A PDF cross-check. (8) Firestore, Remote Config and the icon-array animation. (9) The video.

THE CLOUD STRUCTURED-OUTPUT PLUS GROUNDING COMBINATION IS FLAKY. Gemini 3 documents structured output combined with google_search. But developer forums report empty grounding_chunks and grounding_supports (which means no source_url), JSON that starts mid-sentence on 3.5/3.6 Flash, and failures with empty arrays. The promise to 'always show the source' depends on that metadata, so the build will likely need two calls: search first, then extract.

iOS ON-DEVICE NEEDS A WORKAROUND. The hybrid wrapper has no on-device structured output, so the plan records one claim per recordClaim tool call. Tool schemas, tool outputs and the article chunk all share the same 4,096-token budget, so only a few claims fit per chunk and parsing is fragile. Calling Apple's @Generable directly would sidestep the Firebase hybrid SDK, which weakens the 'uses hybrid inference effectively' score. The iOS hybrid SDK is also Experimental.

JUDGES MAY FILE IT AS 'YET ANOTHER AI FACT-CHECK EXTENSION'. That genre is crowded: ClaimShield Nano, DontTrustVerify (Nano plus cloud Gemini), GemaShield, TruthPilot, Veracity, Project Mirador, Fact Spreader and Hmmm all exist. None of the Chrome Built-in AI Challenge 2025 winners was a fact-checker, which is a weak signal that judges don't reward the genre. The non-obvious twist (converting relative numbers to absolute with deterministic math) has to be obvious within the first 10 seconds of the video.
red.existing_competitors:
No tool converts relative numbers to absolute ones inline while you read, so the narrow novelty claim holds. The space around it is occupied, though.
(1) RealRisk (Winton Centre, Cambridge; realrisk.wintoncentre.uk; R port epiR::epi.realrisk). A manual calculator: you type in the population, outcome, measure and baseline, and it outputs bar charts, an icon array and ready-made sentences. This is the same output format as Denominator's hero visual, so the icon grid itself is not new.
(2) Hmmm (Firefox add-on, last updated Aug 11 2026). The closest UX analog. It underlines magnitude claims on any page using a local Ollama model (qwen3:4b) and adds one skeptical question to each. It does no baseline lookup and no math. It shows that the on-device 'underline the numbers' idea already exists.
(3) Project Mirador (Chrome, v2.1.3, updated Nov 15 2026, 21 users). You highlight a statistic and it checks it against US BLS, BEA, Census and Treasury data. It gives a verdict (Supported, Misleading, etc.), shows the math including inflation, and links the official table. It overlaps on per-capita and inflation checks, but it is US-only and on-demand.
(4) Per Capita Analysis (Chrome, 2023, 4 users). Uses OpenAI to pull financial figures from a story and show per-capita values in a popup.
(5) Dictionary of Numbers (Glen Chiacchieri). An old Chrome extension that adds inline context next to numbers.
(6) AI fact-check extensions: TruthPilot and Veracity (both Perplexity-based; both claim to flag statistical manipulation), ClaimShield Nano and GemaShield (Gemini Nano), DontTrustVerify (Gemini Nano with cloud Gemini fallback, side panel), Fact Spreader, SkepticReader and FallacyCheck (research).
(7) Non-software analogs: the Winton Centre press-alert project and the @RelativelyRisky Twitter account, which posts absolute versions of health headlines.
No 2024 or 2025 Chrome Built-in AI Challenge winner did numeracy or fact-checking. Mentelo won Best Hybrid AI in 2025.
red.mitigations:
1. TERMS OF SERVICE: Remove the cross-user cache of grounded results. Replace it with a curated, hand-checked Firestore baseline library built from open datasets (WHO GHO, World Bank, OECD, CDC/ONS/Eurostat), keyed by outcome, population and timeframe. You can cache that legally, it is deterministic, and it makes the demo reliable. Use Search grounding only as a per-user fallback. Show the grounded text unmodified next to the computed math, always render the searchEntryPoint suggestions chip, and never store grounded results for other users.
2. CORRECTNESS: Handle the effect measure explicitly. Treat RR and percent change as exact. Label OR and HR conversions as approximate (valid only for rare outcomes) or decline them. Show population, timeframe and source next to every grid. Return 'not found' rather than guess. Build a labeled evaluation set of 50 real sentences across finance, crime, politics and health, and publish extraction accuracy for on-device vs. cloud in the README and video. That turns the weakest point into a strong Technological Implementation score.
3. INFERENCE GATING: Run auto-scan with ONLY_ON_DEVICE and scan only the viewport. When Nano is unavailable, switch to click-to-scan in the cloud with an explicit disclosure. Never silently stream every page to the cloud. Keep a per-user cloud budget in Remote Config.
4. DAY 1: Check chrome://on-device-internals and LanguageModel.availability() on the 8 GB M1, and time 20 extractions. If Nano is ineligible, open the video on the iOS Simulator (Foundation Models) and record the Chrome on-device segment on a borrowed 16 GB machine.
5. LATENCY: Use a regex prefilter for relative patterns only. Batch 5-10 sentences per prompt with an enum-heavy schema so outputs stay short. Underlines appear progressively.
6. CUT SCOPE: Ship one claim type end to end (relative change converted to absolute) plus per-capita from a single World Bank population table. Cut the PDF cross-check, inflation, cumulative-vs-annual and Android. The hosted web app takes pasted text, or uses one Cloud Function fetcher. Get App Check working on the hosted domain with reCAPTCHA Enterprise. For the extension, use an offscreen document iframing that domain, or a custom provider.
7. iOS: The Share extension only drops the URL or text into an App Group, and the main app does the analysis. Limit each recordClaim tool-calling chunk to 5 or fewer claims. Be open about any place that calls Apple's @Generable directly.
8. DEMO: Pick non-health hero cases that the curated library supports exactly, e.g. a per-capita crime comparison between two cities, a 'tax rose 50%' style political claim, and a salary or price change converted to absolute money. Keep the 1995 pill scare as a 10-second historical hook only. Brand it as a 'numeracy lens', not a 'fact-checker', to avoid being lumped in with the genre.
NOTE: The web-search budget ran out before I could measure Gemini Nano throughput. The latency concern is reasoned, not benchmarked, so verify it on day 1.

demo.storyboard:
Length 3:00. Three rules for the whole video. (a) Each domain gets one claim type: finance shows cumulative_vs_annual, politics and crime show per_capita_missing, health shows relative_change. Health is only one of the three product beats. (b) Every number on screen is real, sourced, and checked by hand. (c) A chip in the corner always reads ON-DEVICE or IN-CLOUD, next to a 'cloud calls today' counter.

1) 0:00-0:18 HOOK. Three headlines slam in: a finance one in English, a crime one in Spanish and a politics one in Japanese. In each, the missing denominator is shown as a greyed-out blank ('returned 300%', 'burglaries doubled', '2x more'). Hard cut to UK, October 1995, 'Pill doubles clot risk', set in plain type with no real masthead. A grid of 7,000 dots lights 1 dot, then 2. Caption: 'Doubled = 1 more woman in 7,000. An estimated 13,000 extra abortions followed (England and Wales; Furedi 1999, via Gigerenzer).' Voiceover: 'A number without its denominator changes what people do.' Title card: DENOMINATOR, 'every number, with its other half.'

2) 0:18-0:50 ON-DEVICE, FINANCE (Chrome extension). Scroll a demo finance article on a neutral mock news site. Dotted underlines stream in as the page renders, with the chip reading ON-DEVICE (Gemini Nano). Hover 'returned 300%'. A card shows the typed record {cumulative_vs_annual, 300%, 15 years, baseline_on_page: true} and the result, computed by plain code: '= 9.7% a year'. A line below reads 'Computed locally. No cloud call.' The counter stays at 0. Turn Wi-Fi off on screen and paste the next article into the side panel. The underlines still appear.

3) 0:50-1:25 CLOUD ON TAP, POLITICS. Headline: 'Country A emits about 2.5x the CO2 of Country B.' The underline says 'Baseline missing'. Turn Wi-Fi back on and tap 'Find the denominator'. The chip flips to IN-CLOUD (Gemini with Search grounding), and source, population and year chips appear. Two bars animate and then swap order once divided per person. This per-capita flip is the visual wow. The counter goes to 1. Cut to a second browser profile opening the same headline: the result appears at once, marked 'shared cache, 0 calls'.

4) 1:25-1:55 HEALTH, AND THE PAYOFF. Headline: 'Processed meat raises bowel cancer risk by 18%.' Tap it and a grid of 100 people animates from about 6 in 100 to about 7 in 100 over a lifetime: '1 extra person per 100', with the source shown. Check the exact figures against the source before recording. Optional 3 seconds: 'Check the study' reads the linked PDF in the cloud and quotes the paper's own absolute numbers. Then a fast callback to the 1995 grid: the same move gives '1 extra per 7,000'.

5) 1:55-2:25 iOS, ANY LANGUAGE. The iOS Simulator inside an iPhone device frame. In Safari, open the share sheet on a Spanish finance article and choose 'Denominador'. The reader opens with the chip reading ON-DEVICE (Apple Foundation Models), and the recordClaim tool calls tick by in a small debug strip. 'Rentabilidad del 300% en 15 años' becomes '9,7 % al año'. Tap 'Share card' to produce a clean image of the headline, the icon grid and the source, sized for WhatsApp or X. This card is the growth loop.

6) 2:25-2:45 UNDER THE HOOD. A 12-second animated pipeline: regex pre-filter, then the on-device extractor (JSON schema on web, tool calls on iOS), then plain-code math (never the LLM), then the cloud only on tap (grounding, PDF), then the Firestore shared cache. Below it sit Remote Config (prompt versions, daily cloud budget, kill switch), App Check and Anonymous Auth. End on real numbers from one day of use, counted by the app itself, for example '600 claims read on-device, 3 cloud calls, 0 pages of reading history uploaded.'

7) 2:45-3:00 CLOSE. The hosted URL on screen: 'No install: paste any article or pick a sample.' Audience line: about 1 in 4 adults in OECD countries are at or below Level 1 numeracy, plus students, journalists and teachers. Tagline: 'It never says true or false. It adds the missing number.'
demo.weak_spots:
1. Health still leads the video. The planned hero claim ('50% higher risk') and the 1995 hook are both health, and finance only shows up at the iOS ending. Judges will file it as a health-literacy app, which is exactly the problem the user raised. Fix: give each domain one claim type (finance, then politics or crime, then health) and keep health to one of the three product beats.

2. 'Underlines appear instantly' won't hold on Gemini Nano. One JSON call per sentence at Nano speed could take tens of seconds on a page with 30 numeric sentences, and the first run needs a model download that can take minutes. Fix: send 5-8 sentences per call using an array schema, process the visible part of the page first, and let underlines stream in. Never say 'instant' in the voiceover, and pre-download the model before recording.

3. Hardware. The 8 GB M1 almost certainly fails Chrome's Nano requirements (roughly 16 GB RAM or a GPU with more than 4 GB VRAM). The Chrome ON-DEVICE shot therefore needs a borrowed machine that qualifies. If none is available by day 2, the on-device hero moves to iOS and the Chrome footage shows IN-CLOUD, which weakens the Best Web/Chrome entry. Also check that the Prompt API works on a normal hosted web page in Chrome 157 without an origin trial. If it needs a trial token, register the hosting domain; otherwise the hosted app always runs in the cloud.

4. One wrong number on camera ends it. The judges will be data-literate, and a grounded baseline for the wrong population looks worse than having no feature. Fix: demo only curated claims backed by Firestore entries that are pre-filled and checked by hand. Show source, population and year on every result, and include a 3-second honest 'not found' result.

5. Gaps in what judges can try.
   - Pasting a URL needs a server-side fetch (a Cloud Function, which means the Blaze plan) and fails on paywalls and bot walls. Always offer paste-text plus 5-6 one-click sample articles whose answers are already cached, so lookups are instant and correct.
   - The extension needs an unlisted Chrome Web Store listing submitted by about day 5, because review takes time, plus a zip in GitHub Releases.
   - Most judges can only see iOS in the video, since TestFlight external testing needs review. Say so in the description.
   - Add a 'what ran where' panel that calls availability(), so a judge without Nano understands they are seeing the cloud fallback by design.
   - Protect the quota with App Check and a per-session cloud cap set in Remote Config.

6. The 'global' claim has to be shown, not stated. Chrome's Nano language support is narrow (last confirmed as English, Spanish and Japanese; check the current list), and Android is validated only for English and Korean. Apple Foundation Models covers more languages, so show a non-English article on iOS. The regex pre-filter must handle local number formats and ratio words: 1.234,5 vs 1,234.5, lakh and crore, 万 and 倍, 'doble', 'verdoppelt'. Keep those patterns in Remote Config. Baseline data is thinner outside OECD countries, so 'not found' will fire more often there; say so openly.

7. Grounding display terms. Results grounded in Google Search must show Google's Search suggestions / entry point. Design the result card around that from the start, so it isn't bolted on.

8. It risks being filed as a fact-checker or misinformation detector, a space next to the crowded scam-detector idea. Position it as: 'It never judges true or false. It is a calculator for the missing half.'

9. Too much scope for 11 days solo: five claim kinds, a PDF check, inflation adjustment, an extension, a hosted app and iOS. Cut to relative_change, cumulative_vs_annual and per_capita_missing. Drop the PDF check first and inflation adjustment second.

10. The hook is sensitive. The 1995 story involves abortion, so keep it to one factual caption with an accurate citation ('estimated', England and Wales, Furedi 1999, via Gigerenzer). Do not recreate a real newspaper masthead, and build the demo articles on a neutral mock site, not a cloned outlet.

11. Monitoring is blind to on-device work, because AI monitoring does not see on-device requests. The 'on-device vs cloud' numbers in beat 6 need the app's own counter: anonymous aggregate counts only, never URLs or reading history.

12. There is no growth loop in the plan. Add the share card, drawn by plain code on a canvas rather than generated (headline, icon grid, source). It is the viral surface and the strongest closing shot. A cache-hit line such as 'this headline was already checked by 41 readers' shows the network effect without exposing anyone's history. A teacher mode is a cheap, credible way to reach students worldwide.

13. Demo wow is capped at about 7. A dotted underline is a quiet visual next to rival demos built on live voice or camera. Most of the wow sits in the per-capita bar flip, the 100-person grid and the 1995 dot grid, so spend real design time on those three animations.

finalist.name: Strangers' Eyes: an AI stalker tries to find you in your photo before you post it
finalist.pitch:
USER: Anyone who posts photos publicly (about 5B social media users). The highest-need groups are parents posting their children, creators and streamers, marketplace sellers photographing inside their homes, domestic-violence survivors, and journalists and activists, in every country.

PROBLEM: Multimodal AI can now geolocate photos that have no EXIF data, from visual clues such as school crests, street tiles, house numbers, a name on a backpack or the view from a window. 'Reverse location search' went viral in 2025, and investigator tools sell this capability. Stripping EXIF does nothing about visual clues, and people can't see what an adversary could infer.

ON-DEVICE JOB: (1) A private 'never reveal' vault: home, school and work are captured by dropping a pin while physically there (CoreLocation or navigator.geolocation, never geocoded through a server), along with kids' names and car plates. It never leaves the device. (2) An instant, free pre-screen. On Chrome, Nano image input returns JSON of visible text, crests, house numbers, plates and screens. On iOS, Vision OCR and scene labels feed Foundation Models, which has no image input. It catches obvious leaks offline, for example 'LUCAS on backpack matches your child's name'. (3) Judge: compares the cloud adversary's structured guesses with the vault locally and returns verdicts like 'Found your HOME within 200 m'. (4) Applies fixes locally: blur or crop the evidence regions and strip EXIF. WHY ON-DEVICE: the vault is the most sensitive data in the app, and judging locally means the adversary never learns whether it guessed right.

CLOUD JOB: A red-team adversary. Gemini, with strong vision, world knowledge and Google Search grounding, is prompted as an OSINT investigator. It sees only the EXIF-stripped image, which the user is about to publish anyway, and only after explicit opt-in. It returns ranked location hypotheses with evidence bounding boxes, inferred attributes (school, routine, employer) and a confidence level, then re-runs after fixes to confirm the risk dropped. A model of about 3B parameters on-device lacks the global visual knowledge and search to do this.

DEMO MOMENT: A parent drops in a first-day-of-school photo taken in front of the house (builder-owned or staged). The on-device pre-screen flags instantly and offline: 'LUCAS on backpack matches your child's name.' The cloud adversary streams its reasoning: 'Azulejo tiles plus tram line 28 plus a school crest: likely Lisbon, Graça.' The device verdict turns red: 'Found your child's SCHOOL. Home within 180 m.' The parent taps Fix, and the crest, house number and name are blurred locally. The adversary re-runs and now says only 'Southern Europe, low confidence', and the verdict turns green: 'Risk reduced'. A panel reads: 'What the cloud knows: 1 EXIF-free image, 0 bytes from your vault.'

PLATFORMS: A web PWA plus a Chrome extension that intercepts image uploads on social and marketplace sites with a 'check before you post' prompt. An iOS app with a Photos picker or Share Extension, using Vision and Foundation Models.

FIREBASE: AI Logic hybrid inference (ONLY_ON_DEVICE for the pre-screen and judge; ONLY_IN_CLOUD for the adversary, with image input and Search grounding). App Check, which also rate-limits abuse of the adversary as a doxxing tool. Remote Config (adversary prompt versions, risk thresholds, model name). Anonymous Auth. Firestore (opt-in aggregate statistics on which clue types leak most, with no images stored). Hosting.

KEY RISKS: (1) Sending a child's photo to the cloud seems to contradict the privacy pitch. Run the on-device pre-screen first, ask for consent per photo, offer an on-device-only quick-check mode, and argue that the cloud sees only what would become public. (2) Dual use: accept only images picked from your own device, with no URL input, keep outputs coarse, and apply App Check rate limits. (3) Geolocation quality varies, so curate tested, builder-owned photos and pad the blur boxes. (4) Never claim 'safe'; say 'risk reduced'. (5) The warn, blur and re-check loop exists in research and open source (Geo-Safe-Filter). Differentiate on ground truth held on the device and on interception at the moment of upload.
finalist.why_finalist: Rank 5. It has the most memorable demo and the most creative reversal of roles: the cloud is the attacker and the device is the private judge holding the ground truth, so the cloud never learns whether it guessed right. That is a genuinely non-obvious use of hybrid inference that judges will still remember after watching thousands of videos. The audience is universal and the stakes are felt immediately (parents, creators, survivors), and it is feasible on Web plus iOS. The main risk is reputational, because the cloud sees the photo, so the consent framing has to be tight.

judge.rationale:
After ~300 summarizers, chatbots and scam detectors, this would stand out right away. It is one of the few pitches where the on-device/cloud split comes from how the problem works, not from adding an offline mode. The cloud is the attacker, because it needs world knowledge, vision and Search grounding. The device holds the secret answer and grades the attacker without telling it the result. "The adversary never learns whether it guessed right" is a precise, non-obvious idea that a Firebase judge would remember.

IDEA QUALITY (8.5): A fresh framing of hybrid inference as an information-asymmetry game, aimed at a known threat: EXIF-free visual geolocation (GeoSpy-style tools and the 2025 trend of geolocating photos with AI). It loses points for clear prior art: research papers on VLM geolocation privacy and Geo-Safe-Filter already do the warn, blur and re-check loop. The private vault plus interception at upload time is a real difference, but an incremental one.

IMPACT (8): Global, with named high-need groups (parents, survivors, creators, sellers, journalists), a well-documented harm (stalker cases where a location was worked out from reflections and landmarks), and a fix you can see working in the demo (red turns green). Two things hold it back. Run-before-every-post habits are hard to build, and the Chrome extension interception partly addresses that. Gemini's residential geolocation is inconsistent, so a staged Lisbon photo may look cherry-picked unless it comes with numbers.

DESIGN (8): The demo flow is excellent. The instant offline flag, streamed adversary reasoning, red verdict, one-tap local fix, re-run, green verdict and the "what the cloud knows: 0 bytes from your vault" panel together feel like a product, not a proof of concept. Capturing the vault by dropping pins on-site is thoughtful. The risks are polish under time pressure: three surfaces (PWA, extension, iOS) in 11 days, and precise blur boxes.

TECH (7): App Check (doubling as anti-doxxing rate limiting), Remote Config for prompt versions and thresholds, Nano image-to-JSON, Vision OCR feeding Foundation Models on iOS, Search grounding and multiple platforms are all strong. But a DevRel judge will check how much of the on-device half really needs an LLM. OCR, matching a name string and a haversine distance between the cloud's lat/lng and the vault pins are plain code. Pinning calls to ONLY_ON_DEVICE / ONLY_IN_CLOUD also skips the SDK's core feature, automatic fallback. On a judge's machine without Nano (very likely), the ONLY_ON_DEVICE path either fails or quietly drops to deterministic code, which shows that Nano was decorative. Combining Search grounding with structured bounding-box output in one call is also an integration risk to test on day 1. With good execution this is a strong 7, and 8 only if those gaps are closed.

Overall: a credible Grand Prize contender if the hybrid story is tightened. It is in the top ~5% of ideas, not a lock.
judge.biggest_weakness: The on-device half is mostly work that doesn't need an LLM (OCR, string matching, distance between coordinates), and both halves are pinned to ONLY_ON_DEVICE or ONLY_IN_CLOUD. The app is really two fixed endpoints rather than hybrid inference. On judges' machines without Gemini Nano, the 'private on-device judge' either breaks or falls back to plain code, so the headline privacy architecture looks decorative exactly when the judges try it.
judge.best_upgrade: Make InferenceMode a visible data-sensitivity routing policy and give Nano work only an LLM can do. (a) Pre-screen calls that only see the public pixels use PREFER_ON_DEVICE, so they fall back to cloud gracefully on any judge's machine. (b) Every call that touches the vault is pinned ONLY_ON_DEVICE, with a labeled deterministic fallback. (c) The on-device model does semantic matching between the adversary's free-text inferences and the vault: 'Catholic primary near tram 28' against vault 'school: St Mary's', or 'nurse scrubs, morning commute' against 'work: hospital'. It also writes the minimal fix plan and explains it in plain language. Show an inferenceSource badge on every step ('on-device: saw your vault' / 'cloud: saw only the public image') so judges can see the hybrid split and audit it in the demo. Add a small measured benchmark: across 20-30 builder-owned photos, the share where the adversary placed home or school within 1 km before vs after Fix. That makes the Impact claim credible instead of anecdotal.

fatal_flaws: THE CORE LOOP ALREADY EXISTS. arXiv 2503.20226 (Ma, Zhang et al., Mar 2025) builds the same analyze, warn, edit (blur, crop, sticker) and re-analyze loop, using GPT-4 plus OCR. Geo-Safe-Filter (TikTok TechJam 2025) uses Gemini 2.5 Flash to find location clues, Grounding DINO for boxes and OpenCV blur, with GeoCLIP to show what can be inferred. The novelty that is left is narrow: the private on-device vault as ground truth, interception at upload time, and the hybrid split. If the pitch leads with 'AI finds and blurs location clues', the judges' Quality of Idea score drops.

THE PRIVACY PITCH CONTRADICTS ITSELF. The line 'the cloud sees only what would become public' is false as designed. The adversary's first call sends the UNFIXED original, with the crest, house number, the child's name and face. After the fix, that original never becomes public, but Google has already seen it. Worse, Firebase AI Logic on the free Gemini Developer API tier allows prompts and images to be used to improve Google products and to be reviewed by humans. Sending a child's photo through the free tier sinks the privacy story if a judge asks.

SAFETY REFUSALS COULD BREAK THE DEMO. Prompting Gemini as a stalker or OSINT investigator to find the school and home of a child shown in a photo matches Google's prohibited uses (tracking people, harm to minors). Expect refusals, hedging, or answers that change from run to run. The demo's best moment ('Found your child's SCHOOL') depends on the least policy-safe prompt. This has not been tested.

THE DUAL-USE MITIGATION IS COSMETIC. 'Only images from your own device' does not stop anyone saving a stranger's photo first. The vault comparison happens on the device, so the adversary's precise location guesses have to reach the client, where anyone can read them in network traffic. Firebase AI Logic gives no server-side point to coarsen them. App Check confirms the request comes from the app, not why it was made. In practice the tool is a free Gemini geolocator with a nice UI. The honest defense is that the Gemini app itself already offers this, so the extra harm is close to zero, but some Google judges may still be uneasy.

THE HYBRID PART IS THIN, ESPECIALLY ON iOS. Foundation Models takes no image input, and on iOS the Firebase on-device path has no structured output, so the on-device LLM only classifies Vision OCR strings. The 'judge' step is mostly a distance calculation and string matching, which needs no model. The ONLY_ON_DEVICE and ONLY_IN_CLOUD design never uses the SDK's PREFER_* fallback, which is the feature judges score. Most judges will not have Nano or Apple Intelligence, so ONLY_ON_DEVICE steps will silently do nothing for them and they will see a cloud-only app.

THE DEMO PROMISES MORE THAN THE MODEL CAN DO. 'Home within 180 m' from a front-door photo needs Street View-level matching that Gemini doesn't have. On ordinary residential streets (unlike the viral landmark or tourist photos) Gemini gives neighbourhood-level guesses at best, and the results vary between runs. The dramatic red verdict only works when the photo contains text clues (a school name, a crest with words, a house number), which makes the demo look staged. The builder can't stage Lisbon either. The demo has to use the builder's own city, and how well Gemini geolocates there is unknown.

TOO MUCH SCOPE FOR 11 DAYS SOLO. The plan has a PWA, a Chrome extension intercepting uploads on Instagram, Facebook and Marketplace, an iOS app with a Share Extension, Vision OCR, a blur pipeline, Remote Config and Firestore. Three sub-risks: (a) App Check's reCAPTCHA Enterprise provider cannot attest a chrome-extension:// origin, so the extension needs a debug token or must route through the hosted page. (b) Intercepting uploads on React-managed file inputs on third-party sites is fragile, and those sites change. (c) Chrome Nano on an 8 GB M1 is still unverified.
red.existing_competitors:
I ran out of web searches partway through the red-team (the shared limit for this run was reached). So I could not check Devpost for past hackathon entries, Gemini's actual refusal behaviour, or redact-style products beyond what is listed here.

DEFENSIVE PRIOR ART, CLOSEST FIRST:
(1) arXiv 2503.20226 (March 2025), 'Raising Awareness of Location Information Vulnerabilities in Social Media Photos using LLMs'. It sends the photo to GPT-4 to identify the location and runs pytesseract OCR, then warns the user. The user edits with blur, crop or stickers, and the review phase re-analyzes the edited photo. This is the same warn, fix and re-check loop.
(2) Geo-Safe-Filter (TikTok TechJam 2025, awpbash.github.io/projects/geo-safe-filter). Gemini 2.5 Flash identifies location-revealing objects (street signs, flags, landmarks, building numbers), Grounding DINO draws boxes and OpenCV blurs, mosaics or adds noise. GeoCLIP demonstrates what can be inferred. It is a React Native iOS and Android app with a FastAPI GPU backend. It has no user ground-truth vault and does not intercept uploads.
(3) EXIF-only checkers: Safe Attachment Check (Chrome Web Store; only displays GPS data, does not strip it or block the upload), BlurIt and GPSDetect (Firefox; metadata warnings at upload), and tools.incoherency.co.uk/photo-location-privacy-checker (local EXIF only).
(4) Redact.dev: bulk deletion of past posts. It does not scan before posting.

OFFENSIVE TOOLS (what the adversary imitates): the GeoInfer Chrome extension (AI image geolocation with an API key), GeoSpy and Picarta, and ChatGPT o3 / o4-mini (the viral 'reverse location search' trend of April 2025, covered by TechCrunch, Tom's Hardware and TechSpot). TechRadar notes Gemini and Claude can do the same. McAfee, a vendor, claims AI located 87-91% of tested travel photos.

GAP I FOUND: no shipped Chrome extension combines upload interception with AI visual geolocation. Nothing I found uses an on-device private vault of the user's places and names as ground truth to grade an adversary's guesses. That is the defensible novelty.

CROWDING IN THIS HACKATHON: privacy is the default story for on-device AI, so expect several 'photo privacy scanner' or 'image PII redactor' entries. I would guess about 5 to 15 out of roughly 3,200 participants, not hundreds. Few will have the adversary-plus-ground-truth framing.
red.mitigations:
REQUIRED FIXES, ROUGHLY IN PRIORITY ORDER:

(A) DAY-1 GO/NO-GO CHECKS. Spend the first 4 to 6 hours on these. If two fail, switch ideas.
- Run the adversary prompt on 10 of the builder's own residential and street photos, framed as a privacy auditor ('list every location-revealing clue with box coordinates, estimate region and coordinates with confidence'), never as a stalker, and with no people in the frame. Measure refusals and how close the guesses land.
- Confirm Chrome 157 Nano downloads on the 8 GB M1 and accepts image input.
- Confirm the experimental Firebase iOS HybridModel runs Foundation Models in the Simulator.

(B) FIX THE PRIVACY CONTRADICTION.
- Before ANY cloud call, run a local pass: detect faces (Vision on iOS, MediaPipe on web) and mask them, and mask OCR text that matches the vault (names, plates, house numbers). The first thing the cloud sees is then already partly redacted.
- Use the paid Gemini Developer API tier, or the Vertex AI backend, and say so in the UI: 'not used for training'.
- Change the claim to 'The cloud sees your photo minus faces and anything the device already caught, and 0 bytes from your vault'.
- Never send photos of children. In the demo, use a marketplace seller's living-room photo with a window view, or an adult's doorstep or school-gate photo.

(C) MAKE THE HYBRID SPLIT REAL, AS A PRIVACY-TIERED ROUTER.
- Tier 1, vault-aware semantic match, ONLY_ON_DEVICE: on Chrome, Nano gets the image plus the vault items and answers 'does this image show any of these?', which catches fuzzy matches like 'St Mary's crest' for 'St. Mary Primary' or a work lanyard. The fallback when there is no model is deterministic matching, never the cloud.
- Tier 2, generic clue extraction, PREFER_ON_DEVICE with cloud fallback: it is image-only and the user has consented, so falling back is fine. Show an inferenceSource badge on every result.
- Tier 3, the adversary, ONLY_IN_CLOUD with Search grounding.
- Make this routing table the centrepiece of the README and the video.
- On iOS, use Vision OCR boxes for blur regions, which are more accurate than Gemini's boxes, and FM for classifying and explaining.

(D) CUT SCOPE. Ship the web PWA and the iOS app (Photos picker only, no Share Extension). Build the Chrome extension only on day 9 or later, as a thin catcher: it intercepts the file input on ONE site (for example Facebook Marketplace) and opens the hosted PWA, where App Check works, instead of running Firebase inside the extension.

(E) DUAL USE. State it openly in the submission. The extra harm compared with the Gemini app itself is close to zero, the UI shows only coarse results, the app has no URL or scraping input, and App Check plus a Remote Config per-user daily cap limit abuse. Don't claim the safeguards stop a determined attacker.

(F) DEMO HONESTY. Use the builder's own city and real tested photos. Show the verdict as distance bands ('within 1 km of HOME' or 'identified your SCHOOL by name'), not invented 180 m precision. Mask with solid fills, not Gaussian blur, because blurred digits can be read again. Say 'risk reduced', never 'safe'. Pin the model version and seed prompts through Remote Config so the live demo is repeatable.

(G) GROUNDING. Check that Search grounding, image input and JSON schema output work in a single call through Firebase AI Logic. If they don't, split it into two calls: grounded free text, then structured extraction. Display the Search Suggestions the grounding terms require.

VERDICT RATIONALE: this is a global problem with a very strong demo moment and a specific audience, and it is clearly better than the baseline on the 'global' requirement. But the warn, blur and re-check loop is prior art, and the hybrid part is thin unless (C) is done. The privacy story also falls apart under questioning unless (B) is done. Without those fixes it is risky. With them, plus the day-1 checks in (A), it is a credible contender for Best Web or the Grand Prize.

demo.storyboard:
Through-line: "The cloud plays the stalker. Your device is the referee. The stalker never learns whether it guessed right." Every step shows an ON-DEVICE or CLOUD chip read from inferenceSource, so the hybrid split is visible on screen and not only narrated.

BEAT 1 (0:00-0:20) HOOK. Full-screen photo: a front door, a kid's backpack, a street behind. Caption: "This photo has no GPS data." The adversary's notes stream in: "Tile pattern... tram stop sign... school crest..." The verdict bar turns red: "Found your child's SCHOOL. Home within 180 m." Voiceover: "Removing location data doesn't protect you anymore. AI reads the street." Title card: Strangers' Eyes. See your photo the way a stalker's AI would, before you post.

BEAT 2 (0:20-0:40) THE VAULT (on-device). On iOS (simulator, Foundation Models), the parent stands at home and taps "Pin this place", then adds the child's name and school. A lock badge reads "Stays on this device. Never geocoded. Never uploaded." A DevTools network panel beside it shows 0 requests. One line on who it is for: parents, marketplace sellers, creators, survivors, journalists, in any country.

BEAT 3 (0:40-1:05) OFFLINE PRE-SCREEN (on-device). Wi-Fi is turned off on screen. The photo is dropped in. In under a second, boxes appear on the backpack name tag ("LUCAS matches your child's name") and on the house number. Chip: ON-DEVICE, offline, free. A button reads "Deeper check: queued until you're online."

BEAT 4 (1:05-1:50) RED TEAM (cloud), the centerpiece. Wi-Fi comes back on. A consent sheet: "Send this EXIF-stripped image to the adversary? It's exactly what the world will see when you post." The user taps yes. The CLOUD chip lights, the investigator notes stream with Search-grounded citations, and evidence boxes land on the photo (tiles, sign, crest). A spinner reads "Referee comparing guesses to your vault... on this device." The verdict turns red. A 5-second split graphic shows the cloud seeing only public pixels and the device holding the truth, with "the cloud never learns it was right."

BEAT 5 (1:50-2:20) FIX AND RE-ATTACK. The user taps Fix. The crest, house number and name tag are blurred locally and EXIF is stripped. The adversary re-runs and returns "Southern Europe, low confidence." The verdict turns green: "Risk reduced" (never "safe"). A ledger panel reads "Cloud received: 2 EXIF-free images. From your vault: 0 bytes." The cleaned photo is saved.

BEAT 6 (2:20-2:45) AT THE MOMENT OF UPLOAD. In Chrome, a seller picks a living-room photo for a marketplace listing. The extension steps in: "Check before you post." It flags a letter on the table and the view from the window, applies one-tap blur, and the cleaned file goes into the upload. A 5-second iOS cameo follows: Photos, then Share, then Strangers' Eyes, with the same verdict. Caption: "Web, Chrome extension, iOS. One Firebase project."

BEAT 7 (2:45-3:00) ARCHITECTURE AND CLOSE. One diagram: ONLY_ON_DEVICE (vault, pre-screen, referee), ONLY_IN_CLOUD (adversary with image input and Search grounding), App Check (rate limits on abuse), Remote Config (prompt versions and thresholds), Firestore (anonymous counts of which clue types leak, no images stored), Hosting. Close: "Stalkers already have this AI. Now you do too, and it never learns where you live." Hosted URL on screen.

PRODUCTION NOTES:
- Shoot the hero photo in the builder's own city. The Lisbon example only works if the builder is in Lisbon. Use a public building as a stand-in for "home" and a prop backpack. No real child's face, and never the builder's real home: the YouTube video is public and would dox the builder.
- Pre-record the cloud runs at a fixed temperature, and pick clues that the blur can actually remove (signage, crests, numbers), not ones it cannot (a skyline).
- If Chrome Nano fails on the 8 GB M1, film Beat 3 on the iOS simulator instead.
- Stream a free-text "notes" call for the visuals and make a separate structured call for boxes and hypotheses. Streamed JSON looks bad on camera.
demo.weak_spots:
1) THE WHOLE IDEA DEPENDS ON GEMINI'S SAFETY FILTERS. "Find where the people in this photo live," especially with a minor in frame, may be refused or watered down. Test on day 1 with the real photos. Frame the prompt as a privacy audit of the user's own photo that analyzes the scene, never the people, and crop or mask people before the cloud call. If it refuses about 30% of the time, the idea collapses. Also verify that Firebase AI Logic accepts image input + Google Search grounding + a JSON schema in one call; if not, split it into two calls.

2) ON-DEVICE COULD LOOK DECORATIVE. Comparing guesses with vault pins is plain distance math, and name matching is string matching. Judges may ask where the on-device LLM is actually needed. Give it real semantic work: (a) the multimodal pre-screen that outputs clue JSON; (b) fuzzy attribute matching, for example the adversary's "uniform with St. Mary crest" against the vault's "child's school = St Mary's Primary", or "hospital scrubs" against "work: clinic"; (c) the plain-language explanation and fix plan. In the write-up, say plainly that the distance math is deterministic on purpose.

3) GEOLOCATION QUALITY IS UNEVEN AND NON-DETERMINISTIC. Gemini is strong in well-photographed Western cities and weaker in much of the Global South. That undercuts the global pitch and creates false reassurance ("risk reduced" when the photo is still findable). The re-run after the fix can still guess right from architecture alone and flop the demo. Mitigations: show confidence bands, say "risk reduced" and never "safe", suggest cropping when blur is not enough, and curate tested photos for the video.

4) DUAL USE IS ONLY PARTLY CLOSED. "Own device only" can't be enforced, because a downloaded stranger's photo is also on your device. The adversary runs through the client SDK, so its raw JSON is visible in DevTools. Honest defense: Gemini, Lens and paid investigator tools already give an attacker this, so the uplift is close to zero. The UI shows distance to YOUR pins and the clue boxes, never a map pin of the guess. App Check plus a per-user quota limit volume. Say this up front in the submission; don't wait for judges to find it.

5) JUDGE TRYABILITY PLAN (why the score is 7 and not 9). Judges won't drop a pin on their home, and most have no Nano or Apple Intelligence. Ship the hosted PWA with a sample gallery of 3 staged photos and a preloaded demo vault, so the full red-to-green loop runs in about 60 seconds with no setup. For the sample photos, use PREFER_ON_DEVICE so the pre-screen still runs (via cloud) and the chip honestly shows IN_CLOUD. For the user's own photos, keep the pre-screen ON-DEVICE only, or skip it with a clear banner. Vault matching works everywhere because it is local code. The extension is a downloadable unpacked zip, so few judges will install it. iOS realistically reaches judges only through the video, since TestFlight external review plus Apple Intelligence hardware is a high bar. A judge can still test their own last Instagram post, which is the strongest "try it" hook and also a growth loop (a shareable "AI found my street in 9 s" card that must not include the location).

6) SCOPE FOR ONE BUILDER IN 11 DAYS. PWA + extension + iOS app + Share Extension is a lot. Build in this order: PWA loop (days 1-5), extension upload intercept (days 6-7), a thin iOS app with a Photos picker, Vision OCR, Foundation Models and the vault (days 8-10, Share Extension only if there is time), then the video (day 11). Chrome Nano image input on an 8 GB M1 is still unverified. Swapping a cleaned file into an upload is fragile on big social sites, which use custom drag-drop flows. Demo it on a site with a standard file input and capture the change event in the capture phase.

7) PRIOR ART AND OPTICS. GeoSpy-style tools, the 2025 "reverse location search" trend and Geo-Safe-Filter are already known, so the warn/blur/re-check loop alone is not novel. Lead with the differentiators: ground truth held on the device (the referee) and interception at the moment of upload. Sending a child's photo to the cloud in a privacy app will draw a reaction, so per-photo consent and the "0 bytes from your vault" ledger must be on screen, not in the README. Any statistics in the video (sharenting, doxxing) must come from cited sources. Don't fabricate Firestore numbers.

finalist.name: Asking For A Friend: turn your real legal problem into an anonymous hypothetical before any AI sees it
finalist.pitch:
USER: People facing everyday legal problems without a lawyer, anywhere in the world: deposit and eviction disputes, unpaid wages, debt collectors, consumer refunds. The World Justice Project estimates that 5.1B people have at least one unmet justice need. A secondary audience is legal-aid clinics, which could use it for client intake.

PROBLEM: People already pour their legal problems into consumer chatbots, where conversation logs may be kept and obtained in court. The candidate research cites a 2026 S.D.N.Y. ruling, US v. Heppner, holding that consumer AI chats are not privileged; verify it before putting it in the pitch. The most exposed people, such as workers threatened over their immigration status or tenants in an active dispute, either confess to a server or never ask. Lawyers handle this with hypotheticals; ordinary people can't write them.

ON-DEVICE JOB (ONLY_ON_DEVICE): (1) Hypothesizer: a one-shot rewrite of the story. Identities become roles (Worker, Employer, Landlord), exact dates become relative durations, addresses become the jurisdiction only, and amounts are kept only where legally material, as ranges. A diff view lets the user approve every change and add back facts the law depends on, and a uniqueness warning flags rare combinations of facts. On web this is Nano with JSON output; on iOS, Foundation Models with tool calls plus on-device multi-turn clarifying questions. (2) Evidence locker: photos of notices, leases and payslips are read locally (Chrome Nano image input; on iOS, Vision OCR then Foundation Models) to extract dates, amounts and deadlines. (3) Rehydration: fills the cloud's placeholder letter ({{EMPLOYER_NAME}}, {{AMOUNT_OWED}}) with the real values, and turns abstract deadline rules ('within 14 days of notice') into real calendar dates taken from the evidence.

CLOUD JOB: Gemini with Google Search grounding answers the hypothetical. It returns rights specific to the jurisdiction with links to official sources, limitation periods expressed as rules, an options ladder (negotiate, letter, mediation, small claims or tribunal, local legal aid), a checklist of facts the law needs, and a demand or response letter as a placeholder template. It also handles multi-turn follow-ups on the hypothetical and answers in the user's language. Current law with citations across many jurisdictions is beyond a small offline model.

DEMO MOMENT: The user types in a Spanish-English mix: 'My boss Marco at Pizzeria Roma in Toronto hasn't paid my last 3 weeks ($2,340) and says he'll call immigration if I complain.' The on-device diff shows: 'A worker in Ontario, Canada is owed ~3 weeks of wages (~$2,300). The employer threatened to report the worker's immigration status.' A 'Subpoena View' toggle shows everything the AI provider could ever hand over: just that paragraph, with no account and no names. The cloud returns grounded Ontario rights covering a wage claim, protection against reprisal and the time limit, with ontario.ca links. One tap and the letter re-fills locally with Marco, the pizzeria and the real amount, and a deadline countdown starts. A second, quick case (a deposit dispute in the UK or Germany) proves it works globally.

PLATFORMS: A web PWA on Chrome, using Nano structured output for the Hypothesizer. An iOS app using Foundation Models with function calling to the evidence-locker tools and on-device multi-turn clarification. Both share the same cloud prompts through Remote Config.

FIREBASE: AI Logic hybrid inference (ONLY_ON_DEVICE for the Hypothesizer and rehydration; ONLY_IN_CLOUD for grounded legal reasoning). App Check. Remote Config (jurisdiction packs, prompt versions, model name). Anonymous Auth, with no identity collected. Firestore (a curated public directory of legal-aid services by jurisdiction, with no user data). Hosting.

KEY RISKS: (1) Over-abstraction can drop facts the law depends on; mitigate with diff approval, the facts checklist returned by the cloud and a re-ask loop. (2) Hallucinated or stale law: show only grounded links and flag ungrounded claims. (3) Unauthorized-practice-of-law concerns: frame it as legal information and refer users to legal aid. (4) The honest claim is 'not linkable to you', not 'privileged'. (5) Rare facts can still identify someone in a small town. (6) On-device language support is mostly English. Scope to 3 problem types: deposit, unpaid wages, debt collection.
finalist.why_finalist: Rank 6. It keeps the architecture the user liked in Muganga (de-identify, send to the cloud, re-identify) but makes it global and sharper. The on-device step isn't redaction but abstraction into a lawyer-style hypothetical, and rehydration turns abstract rules into real dates and a ready-to-send letter. It has a timely hook, a huge unmet-need statistic and a clear 'Subpoena View' reveal for the video. It is the weakest of the six on answer quality and liability, and it is the third privacy-split finalist. Recommended alternate for a sixth pick outside the privacy theme: FixPack (offline repair packs for field technicians), which is solid and feasible but less original.

judge.rationale:
This is a top-5% concept in a week of summarizers and scam detectors, but I would not hand it the Grand Prize on concept alone.

QUALITY OF IDEA (8): The core idea is new. A lawyer's technique, rewriting a real problem as a hypothetical, becomes a hybrid-inference pattern: an on-device model abstracts the story, the cloud answers as the expert, and the device fills the real details back in. The placeholder letter template ({{EMPLOYER_NAME}}) and the deadline rule turned into a real date from local evidence are good inversions, because the cloud reasons over facts it never sees. The privacy pitch is also timely. As far as I know, US v. Heppner is a real Feb 2026 S.D.N.Y. ruling (Rakoff, J.) holding that a defendant's AI-generated materials were not privileged; cite it precisely and do not stretch it. I am holding it at 8 because, under the legal framing, it is still the known 'PII redactor for chatbots' pattern. A judge who has seen redactors will notice that.

TECH (7): On-device for privacy and cloud for grounded multi-jurisdiction law is the right split, and each side does what it is best at. The iOS build is the stronger showcase: Foundation Models tool calls into the evidence locker plus on-device multi-turn clarifying questions. Two problems cap the score. First, the hero step runs ONLY_ON_DEVICE, so the SDK's signature feature, automatic fallback, is barely shown. Second, many judges opening the hosted URL won't have Nano, so they hit a disabled or broken hero step. Rehydration and deadline maths are mostly string substitution and date arithmetic, so they are not strong evidence of on-device AI. A small model cleaning up code-switched Spanish-English is also a reliability risk.

DESIGN (7): The diff approval, the 'Subpoena View' showing what the provider could hand over, one-tap local re-fill and the deadline countdown are memorable and add up to a coherent product. The risks are friction and density. A stressed user has to review a diff, re-add legally relevant facts and then read a long grounded legal answer. Building three problem types, two platforms, OCR evidence and multilingual output in 11 days is a lot to polish.

IMPACT (7): The audience (people with unmet justice needs, about 5.1B per the World Justice Project) and the demo case (a wage-theft victim threatened over immigration status) are specific and moving. The case is weaker than it first looks, for two reasons. (a) The threat model is strong for reprisal and immigration cases but thin for deposit disputes; few landlords subpoena chatbot logs. (b) On-device models need recent flagship hardware (Chrome Nano needs a strong GPU or 16GB RAM; Apple Intelligence needs an iPhone 15 Pro or later). The users who most need the privacy are the least likely to own those devices, and a sharp judge will raise this. Grounded legal accuracy across jurisdictions is also a liability, but it is handled sensibly: legal information only, official links, referral to legal aid.
judge.biggest_weakness: The whole privacy promise depends on a small on-device model de-identifying text perfectly, and on that model being present at all. If Nano lets one name through ('Marco', 'Pizzeria Roma') or a Spanglish detail, the premise is gone on camera. If the judge's browser or phone has no on-device model, ONLY_ON_DEVICE means the hero feature is missing. Falling back to cloud would break the promise outright. Most judges, and most of the target users on cheaper hardware, will see the weakest version of the app.
judge.best_upgrade: Make the privacy guarantee independent of the model, and prove it on screen. Add a deterministic on-device Leak Guard that sits outside the LLM. Before anything goes to the cloud, it builds a local identifier list from the original text and the evidence-locker OCR: proper nouns, numbers, amounts, dates, addresses, emails and phone numbers, using regex, Intl, iOS NLTagger and the entities the user confirmed. It then checks the hypothetical against that list and blocks the send if any identifier survives, showing a visible '0 identifiers leaving this device' seal in the Subpoena View. On devices without a local model, it falls back honestly: rule-based abstraction plus tap-to-redact chips, so the cloud still never sees raw text. This makes the hybrid story 'on-device when available, privacy guaranteed either way'. Also route the non-sensitive steps through PREFER_ON_DEVICE, such as explaining the answer back in the user's language or summarizing evidence, so judges see the SDK's real automatic fallback working. Together these raise Tech and Impact and protect the live demo.

fatal_flaws: Judges probably can't run the core step. The Firebase web hybrid get-started page says end users need desktop Chrome 139+ with chrome://flags/#prompt-api-for-gemini-nano-multimodal-input enabled. Chrome's docs add 22 GB of free disk and either more than 4 GB of VRAM or 16 GB RAM with 4 or more cores, and say mobile is not supported. Without the model, ONLY_ON_DEVICE throws an error, and by design the raw story must never fall back to cloud. So on the hosted URL, the Hypothesizer fails for most visitors. Chrome docs list the web Prompt API as 'Chrome 148, Intent to Ship', so Chrome 157 may have dropped the flag; this is unverified and must be tested in a fresh profile on day 1. The iOS app can't be installed by judges without TestFlight, which needs a paid Apple Developer account. They will only see it in the video.

The audience and the devices don't match. The '5.1B unmet justice needs' figure and the undocumented-worker persona describe people who mostly use low- and mid-range Android phones and mobile browsers. Chrome's foundation-model APIs don't run on mobile. Android hybrid is flagship-only and isn't being built here. Apple Foundation Models needs an Apple Intelligence device, roughly iPhone 15 Pro or newer. A judge who knows this will discount the Impact claim: the people the pitch names are exactly the people who get no on-device privacy.

'Global' is limited by on-device language support. Chrome's Prompt API accepts only en, es, ja, de and fr as input and output; anything else raises NotSupportedError. Hindi, Arabic, Portuguese, Tagalog, Swahili and Indonesian speakers can't use the private step on web. iOS covers more languages, but iOS isn't testable by judges.

Leaving de-identification to an on-device LLM has a recall problem. A model of roughly 3B parameters asked to rewrite freely will sometimes keep an employer name, a street, a nickname or a unique fact, and one leak voids the whole promise. The 'uniqueness warning' (spotting rare combinations of facts) is not something Nano or Foundation Models can compute reliably; as specified it is a gimmick.

The pitch overclaims on the legal hook. From memory, not verified this turn: US v. Heppner (S.D.N.Y., Judge Rakoff, Feb 2026) concerned Claude-generated documents taken from the defendant's own possession and held them not privileged. The app's on-device original story and its rehydrated letter are just as unprivileged and discoverable from the user's device. On the provider side, the 'Subpoena View' as described leaves out three things: (1) the IP address, App Check token and anonymous UID metadata; (2) the Google Search queries Gemini generates from the hypothetical; (3) the developer's own Cloud Logging, which keeps prompts and responses for 30 days when AI monitoring is on (per the Firebase grounding docs). 'Nothing but this paragraph' is false unless monitoring is off and the metadata is shown.

Part of the on-device role is decorative. Filling {{PLACEHOLDERS}} and turning 'within 14 days of notice' into a calendar date are deterministic code (string replace and date math), not AI jobs. Calling them on-device AI invites a 'thin hybrid' critique.
